articles.title: Next.js 16.3 Instant Navigations: How Partial Prefetching Works
articles.description: Next.js 16.3 shipped Instant Navigations: Partial Prefetching plus the App Shell. Learn the model, the Suspense gotcha, and a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You add a <Suspense> boundary around the slow part of a page, ship it, and client-side navigations into that route still show a blank screen for a beat before anything renders. The boundary is real. It works on the first load. It does nothing on a click.

This is written against Next.js 16.4.2 (verified against the framework's own GitHub release notes and documentation as of October 2026). The fix for the scenario above was shipped as a named feature in 16.3: Instant Navigations, built on two pieces — Partial Prefetching and the App Shell — and it is this series' first look at either.

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain why a <Suspense> boundary that works on a full page load can be silently skipped during a client-side navigation
  • Turn on Partial Prefetching and read what the App Shell actually contains
  • Place your Suspense boundaries where Partial Prefetching can use them
  • Use ensureStatic and the instant dev-time validation to catch a slow navigation before a user does
  • Adopt the feature incrementally instead of flipping one global switch on a large app

Who this is for: you're comfortable with the App Router, Server Components, and basic <Suspense> usage. If you haven't met "use cache", cacheLife(), or cacheTag() yet, this series' Cache Components Explained covers them — Partial Prefetching is built directly on top of Cache Components and requires it to be enabled.

Contents

  • Why your Suspense boundary doesn't help on a click
  • The mental model: three navigation stages
  • Turning it on and reading the App Shell
  • Moving the Suspense boundary to where it counts
  • Per-link prefetching, ensureStatic, and validation
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

Why your Suspense boundary doesn't help on a click

Say you have a dashboard with a shared layout — a sidebar and header that are the same on every route — and a /reports/[id] page whose data takes a second or two to load:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — the wrong way
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params
  const report = await getReport(id) // slow — hits the database directly
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

You already know the textbook fix: wrap the slow part in <Suspense> so the rest of the page can render while it loads.

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — looks fixed
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await params
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
      <Report id={id} />
    </Suspense>
  )
}

async function Report({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const report = await getReport(id)
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

Load /reports/42 directly in the browser and this works exactly as expected: the skeleton appears instantly, the report streams in behind it. But click a <Link href="/reports/42"> from the dashboard's sidebar, and the navigation still pauses — no skeleton, just a delay, then the whole thing appears at once.

The Suspense boundary isn't broken. It's in the wrong place for what just happened. A direct page load renders the whole tree from the root layout down, so the boundary catches the slow Report component exactly as written. A client-side navigation only re-renders what's below the layout segments the destination shares with the current page — the sidebar and header aren't remounted, so nothing above them runs again either. If nothing has told the App Router what to show for the parts of /reports/42 that aren't yet known, there's no shell to paint immediately, and the Suspense fallback never gets its moment on screen.

That's the actual problem Instant Navigations exists to solve: giving the App Router a per-route, prerendered shell to show the instant you click — before the server has even started rendering the parts that depend on the URL.

The mental model: three navigation stages

The mental model: with Partial Prefetching enabled, a navigation isn't one request — it's three separate moments when server-rendered output becomes available to the browser, and each one is cacheable differently.

  1. The App Shell. A per-route prerender containing everything in that route that doesn't depend on URL data — the parts of /reports/[id] that look the same whether id is 42 or 7. This is computed once, like a static page, and served instantly. If a piece of content is cached ("use cache") with a stale time of at least five minutes, it's folded into the shell too; a route that reads cookies or headers gets its session-specific shell cached per session rather than per request.
  2. The per-link prefetch. When a <Link> is hovered, focused, or enters the viewport, the browser can additionally fetch data that does depend on the URL — the actual report with id: 42 — ahead of the click, so it's often already in hand by the time the user commits.
  3. The navigation itself. Whatever wasn't covered by stages 1 and 2 — genuinely request-time work — streams in now, behind whatever Suspense boundary you've placed around it.

Before this feature existed, a <Link> prefetch was all-or-nothing: either the whole destination page was fetched ahead of time (expensive, and wrong for personalized content), or nothing was, and the user waited for everything on click. Partial Prefetching turns that into a staged handoff: shell now, URL-specific data soon, truly dynamic content last — each stage painting something real instead of a spinner.

This is also why the Suspense boundary from the previous section didn't fire: it was in the tree, but without a shell to render immediately around it, there was nothing for the browser to show before the boundary resolves. Fix the shell, and the fallback gets its chance again.

Turning it on and reading the App Shell

Partial Prefetching requires Cache Components (the previous episode in this series covers that feature on its own). Both flags live in next.config.ts:

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
  partialPrefetching: true,
}

export default nextConfig

Key concept: Both flags are opt-in — create-next-app's default next.config.ts ships empty, with neither flag set. Whether your project is brand new or years old, this is the one-time step; the rest of the article assumes it's done.

Turning the flag on changes what a default <Link> does, with no other code changes required. Before, <Link href="/reports/42"> either prefetched the full page or nothing. After, it prefetches that route's App Shell by default — the sidebar, header, and anything else that doesn't depend on id. Setting prefetch={true} explicitly on a given <Link> goes further: it also resolves that link's URL data (params, searchParams) ahead of the click, at the cost of one extra server round-trip per link, which is why it's opt-in rather than the default for every link on a page.

// prefetch={true} resolves this link's own URL data ahead of the click —
// worth it for a handful of links, expensive for a long list
<Link href={`/reports/${id}`} prefetch={true}>{title}</Link>

Moving the Suspense boundary to where it counts

Go back to the dashboard from the first section. The fix isn't a new API — it's placing the existing <Suspense> boundary so the App Shell can be built around it, and caching the parts that qualify:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx — the Instant Navigations way
export default async function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  return (
    <>
      <ReportHeader /> {/* doesn't depend on id — joins the App Shell */}
      <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
        <Report paramsPromise={params} />
      </Suspense>
    </>
  )
}

async function Report({ paramsPromise }: { paramsPromise: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  const { id } = await paramsPromise // reading params here, inside Suspense
  const report = await getReport(id)
  return <ReportView report={report} />
}

The change that matters is subtle but load-bearing: params is awaited inside the component wrapped by <Suspense>, not in the page component above it. Resolving params outside the boundary pulls URL-dependent work above the shell, so there's nothing left for the shell to serve statically. With it inside, ReportPage itself has no dependency on id at all — it's eligible for the App Shell — and the fallback has a real reason to appear: the shell paints immediately, then Report streams in once getReport resolves.

If getReport reads from a cacheable source, add "use cache" to shrink what's left to stream:

async function getReport(id: string) {
  'use cache'
  cacheLife('minutes') // keep this under the 5-minute floor and it won't join the shell
  return db.reports.findById(id)
}

Per-link prefetching, ensureStatic, and validation

Two more pieces round out the picture, plus the path for adopting this on a codebase you didn't build from scratch.

ensureStatic, a route segment config export, asserts that a link's App Shell — and optionally its per-link prefetch too — is actually static, rather than silently degrading. Its values are 'auto' (the default, same as omitting it), 'shell', 'prefetch', 'navigation', and false: 'shell' requires the App Shell to be static, 'prefetch' requires the App Shell and per-link prefetch to be static, 'navigation' requires the entire server-rendered route to be static, and false opts a segment out of a stricter level a parent segment would otherwise impose:

// app/reports/[id]/page.tsx
export const ensureStatic = 'shell'

ensureStatic only works with Cache Components enabled — without cacheComponents: true in next.config.ts, the build fails rather than the export silently doing nothing.

Dev-time validation runs automatically once Partial Prefetching is enabled: Next.js flags a route whose navigation would block on uncached work, points at the missing Suspense boundary, and suggests the fix — exactly the mistake in this article's first example. The Navigation Inspector in Next.js DevTools freezes the page at its initial loading state so you can see precisely what the shell shows before anything streams, which is otherwise too fast to eyeball. If a route is still mid-migration and you want to silence validation for it deliberately, export instant = false from that segment; sibling routes keep being checked.

Adopting incrementally matters on anything larger than a toy app: rather than flipping partialPrefetching: true globally on day one, set export const prefetch = 'partial' on individual page/layout files first, fix what validation flags route by route, then turn on the global flag and run the official codemod to remove the now-redundant per-route exports:

npx @next/codemod@canary remove-partial-prefetch ./app

Edge cases and gotchas

  • "use cache: private" never joins the shell. It caches in the browser only, which is inherently per-user — there's nothing stable to prerender into a shared shell.
  • The five-minute floor is real. Cached content needs a stale time of at least five minutes to be folded into the App Shell; shorter-lived caches still work, they just stream instead of shipping with the shell.
  • A route that reads cookies or headers still gets a shell — it includes the session-specific data rather than being excluded outright, which is easy to assume incorrectly if you've only read about the URL-data rule.
  • router.prefetch() doesn't expose <Link>'s prefetch-depth options. Its public API takes only an onInvalidate callback, not a way to ask for the App Shell versus the fuller per-link prefetch. Reach for it to warm a route outside the viewport, not as a drop-in replacement for a specific <Link prefetch={...}> setting elsewhere on the same route.
  • This is additive to Cache Components, not a replacement. If a route isn't eligible for Cache Components (it has no cacheable or static content at all), Partial Prefetching has nothing to build a shell from, and the navigation behaves as it did before.
  • forbidden() and unauthorized() are still experimental in 16.4. Both remain gated behind the experimental authInterrupts flag and the API reference still marks them as experimental, unchanged since their v15.1.0 introduction. Don't build a 16.4 auth flow around them as if they were final APIs yet.

Best practices

Reach for Partial Prefetching when your app has shared chrome (nav, header, sidebar, filters) that's identical across many routes, and at least some of each route's content is cacheable or genuinely static — the bigger the gap between "shared chrome" and "per-URL data," the more a shell buys you.

Adopt it per-route first, not globally, on anything beyond a small app. The per-segment prefetch = 'partial' export plus the dev validation gives you a route-by-route migration with immediate feedback, instead of flipping one flag and triaging every broken navigation at once.

Avoid it when a route's output is almost entirely user- or request-specific — a live chat thread, a real-time dashboard — where there's little to nothing left for a shell to usefully prerender. The dev-time warning for "Partial Prefetching isn't configured" is a nudge, not a mandate; some routes are correctly dynamic end to end.

FAQ

Do I need Cache Components to use Partial Prefetching?

Yes. Partial Prefetching builds the App Shell out of the same static and cached content that Cache Components makes possible. Enable cacheComponents: true first; partialPrefetching: true has nothing to work with otherwise.

Why didn't my <Suspense> boundary show its fallback during navigation before I made this change?

Because client-side navigations only re-render the parts of the tree below the layout segments shared with the current page. Without a prerendered shell, there's nothing to display instantly above your boundary, so the fallback never gets a chance to appear before the real content arrives — which is exactly what this article's first example demonstrates.

Does enabling partialPrefetching change existing <Link prefetch={true}> usage?

It changes the default (prefetch unset or auto) to fetch the App Shell instead of the full page. An explicit prefetch={true} keeps doing a fuller, per-link prefetch that also resolves that link's URL data — it isn't replaced, just layered on top of the new default.

Is this the same thing as Partial Prerendering (PPR)?

No, though they're related and easy to conflate. Partial Prerendering describes a single route serving a static shell plus streamed dynamic content on one request. Partial Prefetching is about navigation — what a <Link> fetches ahead of a click, across multiple navigation stages.

Can I test that a navigation actually renders instantly, in CI?

Yes — @next/playwright ships an instant() helper built for this: it asserts on the UI that's available immediately after a navigation, so a regression that reintroduces a blocking fetch fails your test suite instead of a user's click.

Cheat sheet

Task Code / Config Notes
Enable the feature cacheComponents: true, partialPrefetching: true in next.config.ts Requires Cache Components; both are create-next-app defaults now
Default <Link> behavior Prefetches the App Shell only No code change needed once the flag is on
Full per-link prefetch <Link prefetch={true}> Also resolves params/searchParams; costs one extra round-trip per link
Keep a page shell-eligible Await params/searchParams inside the <Suspense>-wrapped component Resolving them in the page component itself disqualifies the shell
Enforce a static shell export const ensureStatic = 'shell' No-op (with a dev warning) unless Partial Prefetching is on
Opt a route out of validation export const instant = false Siblings are still validated
Adopt incrementally export const prefetch = 'partial' per route, then the global flag Clean up with npx @next/codemod@canary remove-partial-prefetch ./app
Inspect the shell visually Navigation Inspector in Next.js DevTools Freezes the page at its initial loading state
Regression-test it instant() from @next/playwright Asserts on the immediately-available UI after navigation 
// the whole pattern in one route
export const ensureStatic = 'shell'

export default function ReportPage({ params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> }) {
  return (
    <>
      <ReportHeader />{/* no URL dependency — joins the App Shell */}
      <Suspense fallback={<ReportSkeleton />}>
        <Report paramsPromise={params} />{/* URL-dependent work stays inside the boundary */}
      </Suspense>
    </>
  )
}

Key takeaways

  • A client-side navigation only re-renders below the layout segments it shares with the current page — a Suspense boundary above that point does nothing on a click, only on a full page load.
  • Partial Prefetching (Next.js 16.3+, requires Cache Components) splits a navigation into three stages: the App Shell, an optional per-link prefetch of URL data, and the navigation itself.
  • Where you await params/searchParams decides whether a page is shell-eligible — resolve them inside the Suspense boundary, not above it.
  • ensureStatic, dev-time validation, the Navigation Inspector, and @next/playwright's instant() all exist to catch a non-instant navigation before a user does.

The dashboard from the first section didn't need a new library or a rewrite — it needed its existing <Suspense> boundary to sit somewhere the App Router could actually use it. That's usually true of Instant Navigations adoption generally: the hard part is rarely the config flag, it's finding every place params got awaited one component too early.

articles.title: Your API Timed Out. Did the Payment Still Go Through?
articles.description: A customer clicks Pay.  The screen keeps loading. Then an error appears:  “Request timed out. Please...
articles.body_html:
A customer clicks Pay.

The screen keeps loading. Then an error appears:

“Request timed out. Please try again.”

They click again.

Now there are two requests—and potentially two charges.

Disabling the button helps with accidental clicks. But what happens when the network fails, the page reloads, or a background job retries?

Every developer building payments, bookings, or orders should understand this problem.

1. A timeout doesn’t mean the operation failed

Imagine this sequence:

  1. Your server receives a payment request.
  2. The payment provider processes it.
  3. The response gets lost.
  4. Your server reports a timeout.

The customer may already have been charged.

A timeout means you didn’t receive a response in time. The outcome may still be unknown. AWS explicitly highlights this distinction in its guidance on retries.

Immediately starting a new payment could repeat an action that already succeeded.

2. Give each operation an identity

This is where idempotency helps.

In plain English:

Repeating the same operation should have the same intended effect as performing it once.

An idempotency key identifies a particular operation:

POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 8d5f8ba2-41c9-4a82-a4a2-820897f483f1

If that request times out, retry the same operation with the same key.

Generate a new key for a genuinely new operation.

The key is an identifier. Your backend—or the API you call—must implement the behavior that makes retries safe.

3. Handle duplicates on the server

A typical implementation needs to:

  • Associate the key with the authenticated customer and operation.
  • Store a fingerprint of the request parameters.
  • Claim the key atomically so simultaneous requests cannot both start the work.
  • Track whether the operation is processing or completed.
  • Return the stored outcome when a completed operation is retried.

If the same key arrives with different parameters, reject it.

If the original operation is still processing, return a documented processing response or conflict instead of starting it again.

A “check whether it exists, then insert” sequence alone can race. Use database constraints and appropriate transactions to protect local changes.

4. Protect the payment provider call too

Your database transaction cannot roll back a charge made by an external provider.

Suppose the provider processes the payment, but your server crashes before saving the result. Your local record may still say “processing.”

Use the provider’s idempotency support with a stable key for that payment attempt. Stripe, for example, supports retrying requests using the same idempotency key. Its exact behavior and retention rules are documented in its API reference.

Also provide a recovery path: retrieve the payment’s status or reconcile it through verified webhook events.

While the outcome is uncertain, show “Checking payment status” instead of inviting the customer to start another payment.

5. Retry carefully

Even a safe retry can add load to a struggling service.

For retryable failures:

  • Limit the number of attempts.
  • Increase the delay between attempts.
  • Add randomness to spread requests out.
  • Follow the provider’s retry guidance.

This is called exponential backoff with jitter. It helps prevent many clients from retrying at the same moment.

Don’t blindly retry every error. Invalid input needs correction.

6. Test the uncomfortable cases

Before shipping, test:

  • Two simultaneous requests with the same key.
  • A successful operation whose response is lost.
  • A server crash after the provider succeeds.
  • The same key with a different amount.
  • A repeated webhook event.

For a payment, verify that retries produce one intended charge and a consistent local record.

Apply the same thinking to orders, reservations, credit deductions, and other actions that should not happen twice.

The question to ask before adding a retry

“If the first attempt succeeded but I never received the response, what will this second attempt do?”

If the answer is “charge again,” “book again,” or “deduct again,” the retry needs more work.

A reliable API needs a clear answer for both success and uncertainty.

Have you ever dealt with a duplicate payment, order, or background job? What caused it?

articles.description: I Tried Hono v5 RC: What Changed from v4, and What Breaks?    Will your app break when you...
articles.body_html:
I Tried Hono v5 RC: What Changed from v4, and What Breaks?

Will your app break when you upgrade to v5? Mine did.

TL;DR

With the Hono v5 release candidate out, I set up separate v4 and v5 environments and ran identical code in both. I measured five areas: type checking, runtime behavior, routing, performance, and size.

  • Every type-related breaking change was caught by the type checker. Start your migration with tsc --strict.
  • The real risks are three changes the type checker won't catch: c.json(undefined), the composition of onError() handlers, and changes to wildcard matching.
  • “Smaller” refers to the installed package. The final bundle actually grew by 302 bytes.

Here is the environment I used:

Item Value
Test date 2026-10-18
v4 hono@4.13.13
v5 hono@5.0.0-rc.1
Node.js v24.22.0
TypeScript 7.0.2
Machine Apple M4 (arm64)

Experimental code and raw data

Let me state my main takeaway up front:

The things that break in v5 are the places where v4 was permissive. c.req.json() returned any; c.req.query() concealed the possibility of undefined; and onError() silently overwrote previous handlers. Those were all places where v4's API gave a misleading picture. v5 is simply more honest. Migration may be inconvenient, but that is a different question from whether the design is sound.

This is a hands-on account of testing Hono v5 RC, written for Hono users who want to know what will break when they upgrade.

v5 is a release candidate. Behavior may change before the stable release. Everything here reflects testing on October 18, 2026.

1. Hono v5 Is “Hono for AI”

Before listing breaking changes, it's worth understanding what v5 is trying to accomplish. Once you see that, the individual changes start pointing in the same direction.

At Hono Conference 2026, creator Yusuke Wada described v5 as “Hono for AI.”

He described the goal of AI-friendly APIs as:

Abstracted, with fewer choices.

That was the key to understanding v5.

Changing c.req.json() so it no longer returns any, and turning onError() from a special function that can only be registered once into ordinary middleware, are part of the same idea: remove special cases and reduce the number of ways to do things.

A human might see any and reason, “Well, this will actually be a string, so it'll be fine.” When an LLM writes the code, that implicit assumption may not survive. If the types lie, the generated code can carry the same lie forward.

With that in mind, the changes below make a lot more sense.

2. Setting Up the Test Environments

I completely separated the directories to prevent v4 and v5 dependencies from mixing.

cd sandbox/v4
npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install hono@4
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node

cd ../v5
npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module
npm install hono@next      # installed 5.0.0-rc.1
npm install -D typescript tsx @types/node

The RC is distributed under the next dist-tag. npm install hono@next is the method recommended by the official migration guide.

Here are the actual installed versions:

$ (cd sandbox/v4 && npm ls hono typescript)
v4@1.0.0
├── hono@4.13.13
└── typescript@7.0.2

$ (cd sandbox/v5 && npm ls hono typescript)
v5@1.0.0
├── hono@5.0.0-rc.1
└── typescript@7.0.2

$ node --version
v24.22.0

All tests used app.request() or app.fetch(). Since I didn't start an HTTP server, no runtime adapter was needed.

3. Stricter Types

c.req.json() Changes from any to unknown

In v4, this code passes type checking:

import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()

app.post('/users', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json() // any

  return c.json({
    name: body.name.toUpperCase(), // TypeScript accepts this
  })
})

If a number is sent as name, the code crashes at runtime. The type system provides no protection.

Running the same code through tsc --strict with v5 gives:

src/typecheck-json.ts(9,11): error TS18046: 'body' is of type 'unknown'.

You now have to narrow the type before accessing its properties.

There are three approaches. The first one listed in the official guide is supplying a type argument:

const body = await c.req.json<{ name: string }>()

But this is not runtime validation. The type argument merely declares what you expect. You can still make a false declaration and the compiler will accept it. Personally, I think silencing the error this way misses the point of returning unknown: inspect the value before using it.

The straightforward alternative is a type guard. This passed v5's type checker:

app.post('/users', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json()

  if (
    typeof body !== 'object' ||
    body === null ||
    !('name' in body) ||
    typeof body.name !== 'string'
  ) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Invalid body' }, 400)
  }

  return c.json({ name: body.name.toUpperCase() })
})

In real applications, the third option—using a validator and accessing the validated data through c.req.valid()—is usually the best choice. The official guide recommends it as well.

Destructuring c.req.query() Starts Producing Errors Everywhere

I think this change will affect more codebases:

const { name } = c.req.query()
const upper: string = name.toUpperCase()

const all = c.req.queries()
const tags: string[] = all.tag

This passes on v4. On v5:

src/typecheck-query.ts(7,25): error TS18048: 'name' is possibly 'undefined'.
src/typecheck-query.ts(10,9): error TS2322: Type 'string[] | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string[]'.
  Type 'undefined' is not assignable to type 'string[]'.

Calling query() without a key now has a return type of Record<string, string | undefined>. Consequently, destructured values start producing errors.

The Interesting Part: Runtime Values Are Unchanged

I sent GET /q?a=1&a=2 and compared the actual results.

v4 v5
c.req.query() {"a":"1"} {"a":"1"}
c.req.queries() {"a":["1","2"]} {"a":["1","2"]}

They're identical.

In other words, v5 didn't change the runtime behavior. In v4, looking up a nonexistent key could already return undefined; the types merely insisted it was a string.

Only the types became more honest. Every newly flagged line was already a potential bug in v4.

4. Error Handling Has Been Redesigned

This is the most interesting v5 change to me.

What Changed?

In v4, onError() looked like this:

app.onError((err, c) => {
  console.error(err.message)
  return c.json({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }, 500)
})

There was one handler for the whole app, with the signature (err, c).

In v5:

// Path-scoped error middleware
app.onError('/api/*', async (c, next) => {
  console.error(c.error?.message)
  c.header('X-Error-Handler', 'api')
  await next()
})

// Omitting the path registers '*' under the current basePath
app.onError((c) => {
  return c.json({ error: 'Internal Server Error' }, 500)
})

The signature becomes (c, next), and you read the error from c.error. You can also specify a path and register multiple handlers.

The intention is stated explicitly in PR #5541:

The goal is to model error and not-found handling using Hono's routing system, including middleware composition, path scoping, sub-application handling, and Router-level decoration.

Error handling has been rebuilt on top of the routing system. Internally, the handlers are registered with reserved methods called @ERROR and @NOT_FOUND. That means error handlers are resolved using the same underlying mechanism as ordinary routes.

notFound() now follows the same pattern:

app.notFound(
  '/api/*',
  async (c, next) => {
    c.header('x-not-found', 'api')
    await next()
  },
  (c) => c.text('API resource not found', 404)
)

Measurement: Does Path Scoping Work?

I tested it directly:

Request X-Error-Handler Status Body
/api/error api 500 {"error":"Internal Server Error"}
/other/error (absent) 500 {"error":"Internal Server Error"}

It works: only /api/* receives the extra header, while the common handler produces the final response.

Trying the same thing in v4 yields:

this.errorHandler is not a function

v4's onError() accepts only one argument. It saves the path string as if it were the handler, then fails when a request arrives. Registration itself doesn't complain. notFound() similarly threw TypeError: onNotFound is not a function.

Gotcha #1: Composition Instead of Overwriting

I expect this to be one of the biggest migration pitfalls.

I registered onError() twice and recorded which handlers ran:

Handlers executed Response
v4 ["second"] second
v5 ["first", "second"] second

v4 uses last-registration-wins replacement; v5 composes handlers.

Code that depended on a later registration replacing an earlier handler will now execute both.

When the first handler returns a response, the chain stops:

Handlers executed Response
v5 ["first"] first

Call next() to continue; return a response to stop. These are ordinary middleware rules.

And this won't produce a type error. Once you update the signature to (c, next), tsc passes. You may not notice the behavioral change until you actually run the app.

Gotcha #2: Old v4 Handlers Cause Confusing Runtime Errors

I also wondered what happens if you run a v4-style handler under v5.

First, the type checker correctly stops it:

src/typecheck-onerror-v4style.ts(7,21): error TS2339: Property 'message' does not exist on type 'Context<BlankEnv, string, any>'.
src/typecheck-onerror-v4style.ts(8,12): error TS2339: Property 'json' does not exist on type 'Next'.

It shows exactly what's changed: the first argument is now Context, and the second is Next.

But if you suppress those errors with @ts-expect-error and execute the code, you get:

Context is not finalized. Did you forget to return a Response object or `await next()`?

That message doesn't identify the root cause at all.

These were the arguments I observed:

{ "firstArgCtor": "Context", "firstArgIsContext": true, "secondArgType": "function" }

What your v4-style handler thinks is c is now the next function. It has no c.text(), so an exception occurs and the context never gets finalized. That's why the runtime reports this message.

Suppressing a type error can turn a straightforward migration fix into a long debugging session.

Throwing Values That Aren't Error Instances

In v4, throwing a string or object from a handler could escape past app.fetch().

In v5, the value is wrapped in an Error and sent to onError():

v4 v5
throw 'oops' Escapes outward message: 'oops' / cause: 'oops'
throw { code: 42 } Escapes outward message: '' / cause: { code: 42 }

One detail matters: when you throw an object, message is empty. The original value appears only in cause.

app.onError((c) => {
  console.log(c.error?.message) // '' if an object was thrown
  console.log(c.error?.cause)   // { code: 42 }
  return c.json({ error: 'wrapped' }, 500)
})

If your logs only include c.error.message, you'll be left with an unhelpful empty entry. Check cause too.

Being able to catch strange thrown values from third-party libraries is a welcome improvement.

5. The Most Dangerous Change the Type Checker Won't Catch

The behavior of c.json(undefined) has changed.

v4 v5
c.json(undefined) 200 / body length 0 500
c.json(() => 1) 200 / empty body 500

This is the actual exception thrown in v5:

TypeError: Value is not JSON serializable

The official explanation is that it now matches Response.json(). That makes sense.

The problem is that this does not produce a type error.

If a conditional expression can yield undefined and you pass it to c.json(), you can run tsc as many times as you like and it won't complain. Without a custom onError handler, the built-in handler returns 500, and you might discover the problem only in production.

Of all the migration checks in this article, I would prioritize this one the highest. You need tests to catch it.

One likely example is returning a database lookup directly:

const user = await db.query.users.findFirst({ where: eq(users.id, id) })
return c.json(user) // undefined if no user is found

In v4, an overlooked missing-user case could return 200 with an empty body rather than the intended 404. In v5, it becomes a 500. That means many of the new 500s were bugs already present in v4—v5 merely exposes them.

Another possible case is passing the return value of a void function directly. TypeScript might catch that when the type is void, but it can slip through if any is involved.

6. Wildcard Matching Is Now Consistent

In v4, Different Routers Gave Different Results

I registered the same routes in four routers under v4 and exhaustively checked the matches.

Route Path SmartRouter RegExpRouter TrieRouter PatternRouter
/x*/y /x/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*/y /xz/y ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
/x*/y /x/z/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*y /xay ✅ ✅ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild//card ❌ ❌ ✅ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild/a/card ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

The results disagreed in three of six cases.

For /wild/*/card, only TrieRouter matched /wild//card. In other words, switching routers could silently change which paths matched.

In v5, All Four Routers Agree

I repeated the same checks under v5:

Route Path SmartRouter RegExpRouter TrieRouter PatternRouter
/x*/y /x/y ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
/x*/y /xz/y ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅
/x*/y /x/z/y ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/x*y /xay ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild//card ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
/wild/*/card /wild/a/card ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅

All four agree, matching the table in the official documentation.

The rules are now:

  • A * at the end of a segment is a wildcard; it can match an empty remainder.
  • A * in the middle of a segment, as in /x*y, is not a wildcard.
  • A segment consisting of just * matches one nonempty segment.

The changed results are /x*/y versus /x/y (❌ → ✅ in every router), and /x*y versus /xay (✅ → ❌ for the regex-based routers). These changes also escape static type checking.

Gotcha #3: Adding One Route Changes the Router

This was the most interesting discovery of the whole experiment.

If you register both /x*/y and /x/*, v5's RegExpRouter cannot handle the combination:

UnsupportedPathError: /x/*

SmartRouter catches that exception and falls back to TrieRouter.

I checked which router the app eventually selected:

Registered routes Router selected in v5
/x/* only SmartRouter + RegExpRouter
/x*/y + /x/* SmartRouter + TrieRouter

Adding a single route changed the router used at runtime.

And when I tested those conflicting routes under v4 and v5, even the selected handler differed:

v4 v5
Request to /x/y Handler for /x/* Handler for /x*/y

Routing can change silently, making this difficult to spot without targeted tests.

Measurement: How Much Does Fallback Cost?

A different router should affect performance, so I measured 50,000 requests to GET /users/:id across 12 rounds.

Router Median Mean Minimum
No conflict SmartRouter + RegExpRouter 138.68 ms 152.28 ms 132.35 ms
Conflict SmartRouter + TrieRouter 148.57 ms 163.99 ms 146.25 ms
Difference +7.1% +7.7% +10.5%

The fallback was slower on all three measures.

A disclosure: I reran this benchmark. With just three rounds, I initially measured a 3.3% difference. On rerunning it, I got 8.1%. Three rounds weren't enough for a stable conclusion.

Even after increasing the count to 12 rounds, the raw data contained outliers such as 287 ms and 271 ms (possibly from garbage collection or OS scheduling). I therefore consider the +10.5% difference in minimum times, which is less affected by those outliers, closer to the underlying cost.

Why Would It Be Slower?

According to the official documentation, RegExpRouter compiles registered routes into one large regular expression and obtains a match in a single operation. TrieRouter uses a trie and supports the complete range of patterns, but isn't as fast as RegExpRouter.

SmartRouter defaults to [new RegExpRouter(), new TrieRouter()]. It tries the faster router first, then selects the more general implementation if necessary, continuing to use its choice thereafter. The design is essentially: try the fast one; fall back to the fully featured one if needed.

This test exercised that fallback path, so a performance difference was expected.

With RegExpRouter's consolidated expression, I would expect matching costs to remain fairly stable as routes are added. TrieRouter traverses a tree, so I would expect costs to depend on path segments and the route structure. If that's correct, the 7–10% gap I measured in this small app might be larger in an app with hundreds of routes.

Conversely, in a small application the fallback probably won't be noticeable.

But the exact 7–10% isn't the most important part. The bigger issue is that adding one route can silently switch the router. You won't see that in the logs or the types.

And this might be about more than speed. As shown above, a change in router selection can affect which handler matches. My measurements established that across v4 and v5; I suspect combinations and registration order within v5 could expose related issues, but I didn't test that hypothesis fully.

7. Is It Faster?

I also benchmarked the core routing performance.

Caution: this is an in-process microbenchmark using app.fetch().
It does not represent real HTTP-server or production Cloudflare Workers performance.
It includes no network, TLS, or process-boundary costs.

I ran 100,000 requests to GET /users/:id, with 20,000 warmup requests, alternating v4 and v5 for 10 rounds.

Statistic v4 v5 Difference
Median 270.53 ms 266.50 ms v5 1.5% faster
Mean 278.24 ms 271.85 ms v5 2.3% faster
Minimum 258.31 ms 255.59 ms v5 1.1% faster

My conclusion: the difference is within benchmark noise.

v5 was slightly faster by each metric, but the distributions overlap substantially: v4's minimum (258.31 ms) is lower than v5's median (266.50 ms). This test doesn't justify claiming that v5 is faster.

Benchmarks Without Round Counts Are Hard to Interpret

Another disclosure: at five rounds I measured a 2.9% difference. After increasing the test to ten rounds, it fell to 1.5%.

Same code, same machine, same day. Changing only the number of rounds nearly halved the apparent advantage.

The router fallback benchmark behaved similarly (3.3% at three rounds; 7.1% at twelve).

When discussing single-digit percentage differences in microbenchmarks, publishing the round count and the distribution matters. I learned that firsthand. Every measurement in this article includes its round count.

And unchanged core routing performance isn't bad news. Performance isn't the primary goal of v5's redesign.

8. What Actually Got “Smaller”?

In v5, runtime adapters were moved out of the core hono package into separate @hono/* packages. I expect people to describe that as “making Hono lighter,” so I measured what actually became smaller.

Installed Package Size Really Did Shrink

I queried the npm registry's unpackedSize field:

Unpacked size File count
hono@4.13.13 1.23 MB 574
hono@5.0.0-rc.1 0.66 MB 310
Difference -46% -46%

Running du -sh on my local node_modules showed 2.8 MB → 1.5 MB, also -46%.

Yusuke Wada's Hono Conference 2026 presentation reported 1.29 MB → 0.70 MB, again -46%, with file counts of 574 → 310. The file counts matched exactly. The slightly different absolute sizes probably reflect differences in the referenced versions.

Three independent ways of looking at it produced the same reduction. I think that number is trustworthy.

But the Bundle Got Bigger

Here's the catch: I built actual bundles with esbuild.

Entry point v4 v5 Difference
Core only 18,528 B 18,830 B +302 B (+1.6%)
With adapter 22,760 B 22,923 B +163 B (+0.7%)

It increased rather than decreased.

Thinking about it, that makes sense. The package shrank because the CJS build was removed and adapters were split into separate packages. A CJS build that your bundler never used wasn't contributing to the bundle anyway. And once you install @hono/bun, the adapter code still comes along.

Code previously excluded by tree shaking has simply been separated at the package level. The amount of code ultimately bundled hasn't meaningfully changed.

When saying “Hono v5 is lighter,” specify whether you mean installation size or final bundle size. The first is true; the second was not supported by my measurements.

9. ESM-Only Packaging and Adapter Separation

It's ESM-Only, but require() Still Works

v5 removes the CJS build and becomes ESM-only. The official guide requires Node.js 22.12 or later.

Interestingly, under that requirement, require('hono') still works.

Test Result
require('hono') in v4 OK
require('hono') in v5 OK
import('hono/bun') in v4 Resolves
import('hono/bun') in v5 ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED

Node.js 22.12 and later support loading eligible ESM modules with require(), so using require() doesn't necessarily fail just because a package is ESM-only. The official guide mentions this, and my test confirmed it.

However, subpaths such as hono/bun have disappeared from exports, so those definitely break. The issue is not necessarily CommonJS-style loading; it's the old subpath imports.

All Eight Adapters Were Published on September 28, 2026

I checked their initial publication dates in the npm registry.

Package First published
@hono/bun / @hono/deno / @hono/cloudflare-workers 2026-09-28
@hono/vercel / @hono/netlify 2026-09-28
@hono/aws-lambda / @hono/lambda-edge 2026-09-28
@hono/service-worker 2026-09-28

All eight released version 1.0.0 on the same day. They're the packages split out for v5.

@hono/node-server is not one of these eight. Its first release was on January 7, 2023, and it was already a separate package during v4. Don't confuse it with the newly extracted adapters.

Adapter Separation and Supply-Chain Security

I had heard the argument that separating adapters could reduce the attack surface for supply-chain compromises. I decided to investigate.

On June 23, 2026, Yusuke Wada presented “Hono Supply Chain Compromise Countermeasures: Lessons from Three Libraries” at GMO Flatt Security's meetup on what OSS developers should do about software supply-chain attacks.

The three case studies were axios, TanStack, and Mastra, each with a different attack path:

Library Attack path
axios Social engineering: malware on a maintainer's machine stealing credentials
TanStack Cache poisoning through pull_request_target (“Pwn Request”); possible even without merging the PR
Mastra npm account takeover

Among the Hono-side mitigations was removing adapter functionality from the core. Other measures included:

  • Moving npm publishing from local machines to GitHub Actions with OIDC trusted publishing.
  • Avoiding pull_request_target.
  • Pinning GitHub Actions to lock down the environment.
  • Removing Dev Containers and Gitpod configuration.

This suggests adapter separation is not only about package size; it's also about reducing the attack surface. Size and file count were emphasized at Hono Conference 2026, but the same change had been discussed in a security context back in June.

But It Doesn't Reduce the Dependency Count

Here's something I verified myself.

I queried npm registry metadata for dependencies:

Runtime dependencies
hono@4.13.13 0
hono@5.0.0-rc.1 0
@hono/bun@1.0.1 0 (only hono as a peer)

For comparison, express had 28 and axios had 4 in the registry data I checked.

Hono already had zero external runtime dependencies in v4. Splitting adapters didn't reduce that count. It's zero in both versions.

What decreased was the amount of code shipped in the core package. As shown in section 8, the file count dropped from 574 to 310.

For a zero-dependency library, the package's own distributed code is itself part of the supply-chain attack surface. In that sense, removing adapters is better understood not as shrinking the dependency graph, but as roughly halving the code shipped together in a single package.

10. defineHandler(): The “Fewer Choices” Philosophy in Action

The experimental defineHandler() API is the clearest example of the “abstracted, with fewer choices” goal from section 1. I tried it because it shows where the design is heading.

The simplest example is:

import { defineHandler } from 'hono/factory'

app.get('/ping', defineHandler(() => ({ pong: true })))

ping -> 200 {"pong":true}

There's no c.json(). The returned value is converted into a Response. An object becomes JSON, a string or JSX becomes HTML, and null or undefined produces a 204.

Request and response validation can also be defined in one place:

app.post(
  '/users',
  defineHandler({ json: NameSchema })((c, input) => ({
    name: input.json.name.toUpperCase(),
  }))
)

NameSchema can be anything implementing Standard Schema, including Zod schemas.

With invalid input, I received:

schema ng -> 400 {"error":"Validation failed","issues":[{"slot":"json","issues":[{"message":"name must be a string","path":"name"}]}]}

I ran into one surprise: if you pass an ordinary validation function rather than a Standard Schema and throw inside it, you get a 500 instead of a 400.

invalid -> 500 Internal Server Error

Because the API also accepts validation functions, I assumed failures would be handled identically. But in my testing, only the Standard Schema path wrapped failures into an HTTPException that returned 400. If you need that 400 response, use the Standard Schema format.

And the type definition contains a comment that captures the philosophy perfectly:

A JSON Response by c.json() is not accepted, because it bypasses the response validation. Return the value instead.

Returning c.json() is explicitly forbidden by the types, because doing so would bypass response validation.

This is a shift from “several approaches usually work” to “there's one preferred approach and the types prevent alternatives.” It's a concrete expression of the design goal described earlier.

Note that defineHandler() is experimental and may change before the stable release.

11. Migration Checklist

Here are my priorities based on what I actually measured.

First, Run tsc --strict (Type-Detectable Changes)

  • Direct property access on the result of c.req.json().
  • Destructuring such as const { x } = c.req.query().
  • Treating c.req.queries() values as guaranteed string[].
  • Changing app.onError((err, c) => ...) to (c) => ... and reading c.error.

The compiler will point these out. You can fix them systematically.

Next, Fix the Three Changes Types Can't Detect

  • Any place that might pass undefined to c.json(): it now returns 500. Without tests, this is easy to miss.
  • Multiple registrations of onError() or notFound(): handlers compose rather than overwrite one another.
  • Routes containing wildcards: /x*/y now matches /x/y.

This is the real migration work. Passing the type checker is not enough.

Also look for conflicting routes such as /x*/y and /x/*, which can trigger router fallback.

Update Imports and Removed APIs

  • hono/<runtime> → @hono/<runtime> (eight packages).
  • hono/cloudflare-pages: no direct replacement; migrate to Workers.
  • app.mount() → mount() from hono/mount.
  • app.fire() → fire(app) from @hono/service-worker.
  • c.req.routePath / c.req.matchedRoutes → hono/route.
  • getColorEnabledAsync() → getColorEnabled(c.env).
  • toSSG() hook options → plugins (explicitly include defaultPlugin() when needed).

One small detail: UnOfficalStatusCode was corrected to UnofficialStatusCode. A long-standing typo from v4 has finally been fixed.

12. What I Didn't Verify

I couldn't investigate everything. Here are the remaining questions:

  • Priority of sub-app notFound() handlers when they're integrated via route(). The PR describes deeper-nested sub-apps taking priority, and registration order breaking ties at the same depth, but I didn't test it.
  • How basePath() interacts with onError() path resolution.
  • Benchmarks through a real HTTP server; all my measurements used app.fetch().
  • Performance in an actual Cloudflare Workers environment.
  • Integration of @hono/zod-validator with c.req.valid().
  • Hono CLI 1.0 RC.

And again, v5 was still an RC during testing. These behaviors could change before the stable release.

13. Conclusion

What struck me most was this: the places that break in v5 are the places v4 was too permissive.

The any from c.req.json() and the overly confident string types from c.req.query() gave developers misleading information. v5 stops doing that. The actual query behavior hasn't changed at all. Making onError() composable similarly replaces a special-case singleton with ordinary middleware.

The direction is consistent with “abstracted, with fewer choices.” Even defineHandler() rejecting c.json() through the type system follows the same philosophy.

The migration cost isn't negligible. Fortunately, tsc --strict highlights much of it. The three things to watch most closely are the changes static types don't detect: c.json(undefined), composition of onError() handlers, and wildcard matching. You'll need tests or manual inspection for those.

Performance was effectively unchanged. Installation size dropped by nearly half, but bundle size did not. The reason to upgrade to v5 isn't speed or bundle size; it's a cleaner, more consistent API design.

Would I deploy the RC to production today? No, I'd wait for stable. But running a build of an existing project against hono@next is absolutely worthwhile. The resulting type errors will immediately give you an idea of the migration effort.

Finally, two predictions for the stable release:

If one of these changes gets revised, I think it'll be defineHandler(). It's explicitly marked experimental, and behavior such as “throwing in a validation function returns 500 rather than 400” still has rough edges. Conversely, the onError() redesign and wildcard unification seem well specified in their PRs and implemented thoroughly, so I expect them to remain.

My guess is that the removal of hono/cloudflare-pages will cause the most migration pain. Most changes can be fixed by rewriting code, but this one has no direct replacement and requires a separate move to Workers. c.req.query() may produce far more type errors, but those are mechanical fixes. A single change without a drop-in replacement can cost more time than hundreds of compiler errors.

I'll revisit these predictions when the stable version arrives.

As for my project? It broke, just as expected.

References

  • Migrating to v5 — Hono — Official breaking-change guide; the source for my test cases.
  • feat!: add routable error and not-found middleware (honojs/hono#5541) — onError() / notFound() redesign, reserved route methods, and sub-app priority rules.
  • Hono Conference 2026 — Yusuke Wada — The “Hono for AI” framing and package size figures.
  • honojs/hono releases — Release dates of 5.0.0-rc.0 (2026-10-08) and 5.0.0-rc.1 (2026-10-10).
  • Hono Supply Chain Compromise Countermeasures — Yusuke Wada — Case studies of axios, TanStack, and Mastra; adapter extraction as a mitigation. (Japanese)
  • “What Should OSS Developers Do Now?” meetup report — kouki_engineer — Attendee report on the June 23, 2026 GMO Flatt Security meetup. (Japanese)
  • npm registry: hono — Source for dependencies, unpackedSize, and fileCount.
  • Standard Schema — Common schema interface accepted by defineHandler().
  • Routers — Hono — RegExpRouter, TrieRouter, SmartRouter, and default selection.
  • Mount Middleware — Hono — Migration destination for the removed app.mount().

articles.title: Is Claude taking control of my development skills? I went looking for proof.
articles.description: Last Tuesday I hit a bug. A React component was rendering stale data. Two years ago, I'd have known...
articles.body_html:
Last Tuesday I hit a bug. A React component was rendering stale data. Two years ago, I'd have known the problem on sight.

This time, my hand moved before my brain did. I selected the code, hit my Claude shortcut, and typed "fix this."

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(() => {
    setCount(count + 1);   // always 0 + 1. classic stale closure.
  }, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);   // empty deps = count is frozen at its first value

Claude fixed it in four seconds. Used the functional update, setCount(c => c + 1). I hit accept and moved on.

Then I stopped, because something felt off. I hadn't solved anything. I'd pattern-matched "bug" → "ask Claude" and skipped the part in the middle, the part where I used to actually understand what was broken. That's a bug I'd explained to junior devs a dozen times. And I'd just outsourced it without a thought.

So I asked myself the honest question: is Claude quietly taking my skills? And instead of answering with a gut feeling, I went and read the actual research. Here's what I found, including a study from Anthropic itself, and the one habit that fixed it for me.

It's not man vs machine. It's a quieter thing.

"Taking control" sounds dramatic. The truth is boring and worse: it's cognitive offloading. When you hand a mental task to a tool, your brain does less of the work. And the work is the skill.

You already know this from real life:

  • GPS. A 2017 Nature study put people through virtual London streets. The ones following turn-by-turn directions showed measurably less activity in the hippocampus, the brain's map-maker, than people navigating on their own. Offload the navigating, and the navigating muscle goes quiet.
  • The gym. A forklift moves the weight faster than you ever could. That's not the point. Lifting it yourself is the point.

Claude is a forklift for code. Incredible leverage. And if I let it lift everything, I stop being able to lift anything.

The question is whether coding this way does to my debugging what GPS does to your sense of direction. Turns out, people have measured it.

Proof #1: You feel faster. You're measurably slower.

This is the one that rattled me, because it attacks the thing I trust most, my own read on how a session went.

Researchers at METR ran a proper experiment in early 2025. 16 experienced open-source developers. 246 real tasks in repos they already maintained. Half the tasks: AI allowed (Cursor + Claude). Half: AI forbidden. Then they measured the clock.

  • Before starting, the devs guessed AI would make them 24% faster.
  • After finishing, they felt it had made them about 20% faster.
  • The stopwatch said they were 19% slower with AI.

Sit with that. They were slower, and they couldn't feel it. A ~39-point gap between how fast they felt and how fast they were.

That's the dangerous part. A skill you're losing while feeling more productive is a skill you'll never catch yourself losing.

(Honest caveat: small sample, and METR says it doesn't generalize to all work. But the perception gap is the scary bit, and it matches everything below.)

Proof #2: Anthropic studied its own tool. The result is brutal and fair.

This is the study that actually changed how I work. And it's remarkable because it comes from the company that makes Claude.

They took 52 developers learning Trio (a Python async library, new to all of them). One group coded with an AI that could hand them correct code on request. The other group hand-coded. Then everyone took a quiz, debugging, reading code, writing code, concepts, on stuff they'd used ten minutes earlier.

  • Hand-coders averaged 67%.
  • AI-assisted averaged 50%. Seventeen points lower. Nearly two letter grades.
  • The AI group saved about two minutes. Not even a statistically real difference.
  • The biggest gap was on debugging — the exact skill you need the second the AI's code breaks.

So the trade was: two letter grades of understanding, for two meaningless minutes. That's the trade I'd been making on autopilot in my useEffect.

But here's the part that saved me from just rage-quitting Claude: it wasn't the AI that did the damage. It was how they used it.

The devs who bombed the quiz (under 40%) were the ones doing pure delegation, "write this for me," dump the error in, take the fix. The devs who aced it (65%+) were the ones asking Claude to explain — generate, then understand; ask "why this approach"; work through the error themselves.

And the explainers weren't slow. Asking conceptual questions was the second-fastest pattern in the whole study.

You don't have to choose between shipping and learning. You have to choose between delegating and understanding. And in the moment, those two feel almost identical.

The difference is literally how you type the prompt

This is the whole article in one example. Same bug, two prompts.

❌ The prompt that deskills me:

fix this

I paste code, I get a diff, I hit accept. I learned nothing. My brain logged "handled," not "here's why."

✅ The prompt that teaches me:

This useEffect shows stale data. Don't rewrite it yet —
explain WHY the count is frozen, then show me two ways to fix it
and the tradeoff between them.

Now Claude tells me it's a stale closure: the effect captured count at its first value and the empty dependency array froze it there. It shows me setCount(c => c + 1) (functional update) and adding count to the deps (re-subscribes the interval), and explains why the functional update is usually better here.

Same four seconds. Same correct answer. Completely different outcome in my head. One makes Claude my hands. The other makes it my senior engineer who explains while we work.

That's not a philosophy. That's the Anthropic data: the first prompt scored ~38%, the second scored ~70%.

Proof #3: You can see it in the commits

If skills are quietly eroding across the industry, you'd expect it to show up in the code we actually ship. It does.

GitClear studied 211 million changed lines from 2020 to 2024, right across the window AI assistants went mainstream.

  • 2024 was the first year on record where copy-pasted code beat refactored (moved) code. We're pasting more than we're consolidating.
  • Refactoring fell off a cliff — "moved" lines dropped from ~25% (2021) to under 10% (2024).
  • Duplicated blocks (5+ identical lines) jumped roughly 8x in 2024.

It's correlational, not a smoking gun. But it lines up: AI makes it trivial to insert a block and rarely nudges you to reuse what's already there. The codebase gets fatter. And the understanding of why it's shaped that way lives nowhere, because nobody wrote it, Claude did, and you accepted it.

There's even a name for this now: Knowledge Debt — technical debt's quieter cousin that lives in your head instead of the repo. Every "accept" on code you didn't understand is a withdrawal.

Let me be fair: the other side is real too

I'm not here to tell you to delete Claude. That'd be stupid, and dishonest.

  • These studies are early and small. Anthropic's devs were learning a new library — that's not the same as a senior engineer forgetting what they know.
  • Deskilling is a slope, not a cliff. You don't wake up unable to code. You slowly stop reaching for a skill until it's rusty. Which means you can catch it.
  • The leverage is genuinely incredible. I've shipped entire projects with Claude I'd never have attempted solo. That's not a small thing.

The evidence doesn't say "AI makes you worse." It says "AI makes you worse if you let it do the thinking, and better if you make it do the explaining." That line is the entire game.

My field guide: using Claude without going soft

Here's what I actually changed. Concrete rules, not vibes.

1. The 10-second rule. Before I paste a bug into Claude, I give myself 10 seconds to say out loud what I think is wrong. Even a guess. Then I ask Claude. Half the time I was right and just lazy. The other half, now I'm actually learning instead of skipping.

2. "Explain, don't just fix." My default debugging prompt is now literally:

Explain why this is broken before you fix it.

Five words. Keeps me in the loop. Keeps the senior engineer, loses the vending machine.

3. Read the diff like it's a PR from a junior. Would I approve this in review? If I can't say why it works, I don't accept it, I ask, or I rewrite it.

4. One hard thing a week, cold. Once a week I take a real problem and solve it with Claude closed. It's slower and slightly humbling. That's the gym. The slowness is the whole point.

Here's the split I try to stay on the right side of:

❌ Erodes the skill ✅ Builds the skill
Accept the diff without reading it Read it, then accept
"Write this feature for me" "Explain the approach, then I'll write it"
Paste the error, take the fix Guess first, then compare with Claude
Trust it because it compiles Verify it because you understand it
Let it refactor code you don't grasp Refactor it yourself, ask Claude to review

Every single row is the same choice: delegation vs understanding. The left column cost those developers two letter grades. The right column cost them almost nothing but a little friction.

So, is Claude taking control?

No. And honestly, that's worse.

Claude isn't taking anything. I'm handing it over, one frictionless "accept" at a time, feeling more productive the whole way down, which is exactly how the METR study says it would feel.

The tool just amplifies whatever I bring to it. Bring laziness, and it deskills me with terrifying efficiency. Bring curiosity, make it explain, guess before I ask, verify every diff, and it becomes the best mentor I've ever had, available at 2am, infinitely patient, never annoyed at the dumb question.

The skill I actually have to protect isn't React, or async, or debugging. It's the judgment to know when to let Claude think for me and when to make myself do it. That's the one thing I can't outsource, because the moment I do, there's nobody left to make the call.

I'm keeping Claude. I'm just not closing my eyes anymore.

Sources (all with caveats noted inline above): METR RCT on experienced-developer productivity (16 devs, 246 tasks); Anthropic, "How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills" (52 devs, 50% vs 67%, Cohen's d=0.738, p=0.01); GitClear 2025 AI Code Quality report (211M lines); MIT Media Lab, "Your Brain on ChatGPT" (arXiv:2506.08872, not peer-reviewed); Nature Communications (2017) on GPS and hippocampal activity. Several are preprints or correlational.

Quick gut-check before the comments: last time you asked Claude to fix something, did you type "fix this" or "explain why it's broken"? Be honest. That answer is the whole study, run on a sample size of you. 👇

articles.title: The File Format: Pages, Headers, and Magic Bytes
articles.description: Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 2  The first article was about the why. This one is where things get...
articles.body_html:
Series: nosqlite devlog, Part 2

The first article was about the why. This one is where things get concrete.

I remember the exact moment I opened a hex editor on a SQLite file for the first time. The first 16 bytes said 53 51 4C 69 74 65 20 66 6F 72 6D 61 74 20 33 00. That decodes to SQLite format 3. A literal string. Right there at byte zero. Before any data, before any tables, before anything useful, the file just tells you what it is.

I thought that was brilliant. And I knew immediately that nosqlite would need the same thing.

When you open a nosqlite database for the first time, the file does not exist yet. The code creates it. But it does not just create a blank file and start dumping data. It sets up a structure. A layout. A way of knowing where everything is and what it means.

This is the file format.

Why Structure Matters

Imagine a file that contains two documents, both stored as raw BSON bytes, one after another. How do you know where the first document ends and the second begins? How do you know if the file is a valid nosqlite database and not a corrupted archive or a random binary blob? How do you find a specific document without reading everything from byte zero?

You cannot answer any of those questions without structure.

Every database engine, from SQLite to PostgreSQL to LevelDB, has a defined file format. It is as much a part of the project as the code itself. nosqlite is no different.

The Page: The Fundamental Unit

The core abstraction in nosqlite is the page. A page is a fixed-size block of bytes, exactly 4096 bytes. This number is not arbitrary.

Most modern operating systems use a memory page size of 4096 bytes. When you read a file, the OS reads it in chunks that align to this boundary. If your database reads in 4096-byte units, you are playing along with the OS instead of fighting it. One read operation brings in exactly one page.

Here is how the page is defined in the code:

pub const PAGE_SIZE: usize = 4096;
pub const PAGE_HEADER_SIZE: usize = 16;

#[repr(u8)]
pub enum PageType {
    Free = 0,
    CollectionCatalog = 1,
    CollectionData = 2,
}

Every page has a header that occupies the first 16 bytes. The rest of the page is available for data. The page type tells the engine what kind of data is in this page. Right now there are three types: a free page (not in use), a catalog page (which tracks collections), and a data page (which holds actual documents).

That enum attribute #[repr(u8)] is a Rust thing worth understanding. It tells the compiler to represent the enum as a single byte. This matters because this value gets written directly into the file. When you read that byte back, you can determine what kind of page you are looking at.

The File Header

The very first thing in a nosqlite database file is the file header. It lives in the first 4096 bytes, which is a full page. Even though it does not fill all 4096 bytes, it reserves the entire first page so that page numbering is consistent. Page 0 is always the header.

pub const FILE_HEADER_SIZE: u64 = 4096;
pub const MAGIC_BYTES: &[u8; 16] = b"NOSQLITE_DB___P8";

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct FileHeader {
    pub version: u32,
    pub total_pages: u64,
    pub free_list_head: u64,
    pub catalog_page: u64,
}

Take a look at MAGIC_BYTES. This 16-byte sequence is the first thing written into every nosqlite database file. When you open a file, the very first check is: do these first 16 bytes match? If they do not, this is not a nosqlite database, and the engine refuses to proceed.

This is called a magic number or magic bytes. Every well-designed binary format has one. PNG files start with \x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n. ZIP files start with PK. SQLite files start with SQLite format 3. The magic bytes let any reader quickly identify the format before attempting to parse anything.

The P8 at the end is personal. It is a nod to p8labs, my own project namespace. Every file this engine creates carries that marker.

What the Header Tracks

The FileHeader struct holds four pieces of information:

version is a u32 that identifies the format version. This is future-proofing. If the file format changes in a breaking way, the version number changes too. An older reader can detect that the format is newer than it understands and refuse gracefully.

total_pages is a u64 counting how many pages exist in the file right now. Every time a new page is allocated, this counter increments.

free_list_head is a u64 holding the page number of the first free page. When you delete a collection or its documents, those pages do not disappear from the file. They go onto a linked list of free pages. Next time you need a new page, you can reuse one from this list instead of growing the file. This is 0 when there are no free pages.

catalog_page is a u64 holding the page number of the catalog page. The catalog is where the list of all collections is stored. You need to know where it is to do anything useful.

Binary Encoding

The file header and every other structure in nosqlite is encoded in little-endian format. Little-endian means the least-significant byte comes first.

For example, the number 1 as a u32 in little-endian is 01 00 00 00. In big-endian it would be 00 00 00 01. Most consumer hardware (x86, ARM in modern Linux defaults) is little-endian, which is why most database formats choose it.

The codec module handles reading and writing these values:

pub fn read_u32(buffer: &[u8], cursor: &mut usize) -> Result<u32> {
    let bytes = buffer.get(*cursor..*cursor + 4).ok_or(Error::Corruption)?;
    *cursor += 4;
    Ok(u32::from_le_bytes(
        bytes.try_into().map_err(|_| Error::Corruption)?,
    ))
}

pub fn read_u64(buffer: &[u8], cursor: &mut usize) -> Result<u64> {
    let bytes = buffer.get(*cursor..*cursor + 8).ok_or(Error::Corruption)?;
    *cursor += 8;
    Ok(u64::from_le_bytes(
        bytes.try_into().map_err(|_| Error::Corruption)?,
    ))
}

The cursor is a mutable reference to a position. Each read_* call advances the cursor by the number of bytes consumed. This pattern makes sequential reading clean. You start the cursor at 0, call read_u16, then read_u32, then read_u64, and the cursor tracks your position through the buffer automatically. No manual offset arithmetic.

The ok_or(Error::Corruption) at the end is the defensive part. If the buffer is shorter than expected, the engine returns a Corruption error instead of panicking. In a storage engine, unexpected short reads almost always mean the file has been truncated or corrupted. Detecting this rather than crashing is the correct behavior.

The Pager

The structure that manages all page reads and writes is called the Pager. This is a concept borrowed directly from SQLite's architecture.

pub struct Pager {
    file: File,
    pub header: FileHeader,
}

impl Pager {
    pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<Self> {
        let mut file = OpenOptions::new()
            .create(true)
            .read(true)
            .write(true)
            .open(path)?;

        let header = if file.metadata()?.len() == 0 {
            Self::initialize_database(&mut file)?
        } else {
            read_header(&mut file)?
        };
        Ok(Self { file, header })
    }
    // ...
}

When you call Pager::open, it either initializes a fresh database or reads the existing header. The check is simple: if the file length is 0, the file is brand new and needs to be set up. Otherwise, read the header and trust that the rest of the file is structured correctly.

The OpenOptions call is standard Rust file I/O. create(true) means create the file if it does not exist. read(true) and write(true) give the handle both read and write permissions.

The Pager is the only thing in the codebase that directly interacts with the file. Every other module that needs to read or write pages goes through the Pager. This is important for correctness. Centralizing file access means page reads and writes are consistent. In the future, caching pages in memory before writing them to disk will happen inside the Pager, without touching anything else.

Bootstrap: First Database Write

When initialize_database runs on a fresh file, it does a few things:

It writes the magic bytes at byte 0. It writes an initial FileHeader. It allocates the first real page (page 1) as the catalog page and initializes it. It updates the header to point catalog_page at 1. Then it flushes everything to disk.

After that, the file is a valid nosqlite database with no collections and no documents, but with the infrastructure in place to hold them.

On every subsequent open, the Pager reads the header, verifies the magic bytes, and trusts the structure. Nothing needs to be rebuilt.

The File Layout So Far

Here is what the file looks like after initialization:

Byte 0       : NOSQLITE_DB___P8   (16 bytes, magic)
Byte 16      : version             (u32, 4 bytes)
Byte 20      : total_pages         (u64, 8 bytes)
Byte 28      : free_list_head      (u64, 8 bytes)
Byte 36      : catalog_page        (u64, 8 bytes)
Byte 44-4095 : padding / reserved
Byte 4096    : Catalog page header (16 bytes)
Byte 4112+   : Catalog page data

This is the foundation. Every feature built on top of nosqlite reads and writes through this structure.

In the next article, we look at collections. What is a collection in a NoSQL database? How does the catalog page know what collections exist and where their documents live? What happens at the byte level when you create a collection or delete one?

That is where the data starts to feel real.
