articles.title: Every DIY Project Starts as Automation and Ends as Art
articles.description: We tell ourselves we're optimizing. What we're really doing is leaving fingerprints on...
articles.body_html:
We tell ourselves we're optimizing. What we're really doing is leaving fingerprints on silicon.

You know the lie.

It starts in the most reasonable way possible. You have a problem that is objectively stupid and therefore must be solved.

"The fern is dying."
"The light switch is too far."
"The mailbox doesn't tell me when there's mail."

And you, being a person who knows what an ESP32 is, think: I can automate that.

This is how it begins. Every time. A clean, utilitarian, defensible justification for ordering another dev board you absolutely do not need.

I have a drawer full of these justifications. None of them ended as automation.

Phase 1: The Automation Delusion

The automation phase is pure engineer brain. It's elegant. It's logical. It's a lie.

You open Arduino IDE — or PlatformIO if you've seen the light — and you write the most honest code you'll ever write in the project:
Beautiful. Simple. Utilitarian. You could put this on a resume.

You wire up an ESP32, a capacitive soil sensor, a tiny pump. You flash it. It works. For exactly 47 minutes. Then the sensor corrodes, the pump clogs, the ESP32 decides it no longer likes your Wi-Fi password, and your fern is somehow more dead than before.

This is the first lesson hardware teaches you that software never will: Hardware doesn't care about your intentions. It cares about physics.

Your code can be perfect. Your solder joint can still be cold. Your 3.3V rail can still sag when the pump kicks on and brown-out the whole board. Your "low power deep sleep" is pulling 80mA because you left the power LED on like an amateur.

Software forgives. Hardware remembers.

And yet, we stay. Why?

Because somewhere between the third time you re-solder that header and the first time your janky prototype actually waters the plant by itself, something shifts.

You stop caring about whether the fern lives.

Phase 2: The Creep

This is the phase no one talks about on YouTube tutorials. The scope creep that isn't about features. It's about feel.

You got it to water the plant. Automation: complete. You should be done.

But the bare PCB on the soil looks sad. So you design a little enclosure. Just a simple box in Fusion 360. 30 minutes, tops.

Four hours later you are debating 0.2mm vs 0.16mm layer height, whether matte black PETG says "I am a serious adult who waters plants" and if you should add a tiny embossed fern leaf on the lid because... why not?

Then you think: the LED is too harsh. It should fade in slowly, like a sunrise, when it waters. Not just blink. Breathe.

So you rewrite digitalWrite() into a PWM fade loop with an ease-in-out curve you copied from a frontend animation library. For a plant. A plant does not care about easing functions.

Then you add an OLED. Just to show moisture percentage. Then you add a little animation of a happy fern when moisture is good and a droopy fern when it's not. You spend a whole evening drawing 8x8 pixel art ferns.

You came to automate. You stayed to anthropomorphize.

This is the moment every DIY project crosses the line from engineering into art. You are no longer solving the problem. You are expressing how you feel about the problem.

Automation asks: "Does it work?"
Art asks: "Does it feel like me?"

Phase 3: Why The ESP32 Made Us All Artists

The old Arduino Uno was honest. It had 32KB of flash. It could barely hold your code and a grudge. It kept you humble. You built what you needed because you had to.

The ESP32-S3 is a dangerous thing. It's a $7 supercomputer that pretends to be a microcontroller. Dual core 240MHz, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, 8MB PSRAM, camera interface, Touch, Hall sensor, stuff you'll never use but love knowing is there.

It has so much headroom that you stop asking "Can I do this?" and start asking "What if I did this beautifully?"

That's why an ESP32 project never ends. There's always one more peripheral. One more sensor. One more ridiculous idea that the chip can absolutely handle, even if you can't.

You start with a mailbox sensor. You end with a mailbox that sends you a Telegram message with a haiku about the mailman, logs the temperature and humidity inside the box, and plays the Metal Gear Solid alert sound when junk mail arrives.

Is that automation? No. Is that necessary? Absolutely not. Is it yours? Completely.

We used to buy objects that were made for us. Now, for the first time in industrial history, normal people can make objects that are like us. Flawed, over-engineered, weirdly sentimental, with inside jokes baked into the firmware.

My house is full of objects that don't make sense to anyone else. A light that turns warm when it rains because I like rainy days. A switch that needs to be double-tapped because single taps are too impatient. A little desktop friend that just sits there and blinks at me when my build fails.

None of these automate anything. All of them make the place feel inhabited.

The Real Circuit

Here's what I actually think after a decade of burning my fingers with a soldering iron that was definitely off:

We tell ourselves we are building smart homes, but we are building haunted homes. Not haunted by ghosts, but haunted by our own attention.

Every time you choose a warm white LED over a cool white one, every time you tune a sensor threshold by hand, every time you add a silly little animation that only you will ever see — you are leaving a fingerprint in the machine.

The big tech companies are trying to make devices that work for everyone. We are making devices that work for one person. That's not a bug. That's the entire point.

Automation is the excuse we give our partners and our wallets. Art is the reason we actually do it at 1 AM on a Tuesday.

So the next time your "simple automatic plant waterer" has a custom PCB, a web dashboard you designed from scratch, and a name — you didn't fail at keeping scope small.

You succeeded at making something human.

You started as an engineer trying to save a fern. You ended as an artist who gave a fern a little robot guardian that breathes.

And honestly? The fern is still going to die. But what a way to go.

If this hit, you'll want what's on my workbench:

I turn these late-night spirals into buildable field kits. No cloud, no subscriptions, just hardware that feels like yours.

1. Hardware Signals Field Pack — ESP32 & Sub-GHz RF Research Lab
The lab I wish I had when I started. ESP32-S3 + CC1101 BOM, portable listening platform, real-world RF capture workflows, and the glue scripts so you stop re-writing the same Python parser for the 100th time. Build a defensive tool you can actually carry.
→ numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/hardwaresignals

2. ESP32 Phantom Networks — Portable Mesh & Offline Infrastructure
For when your art wants to leave the house. How to get ESP32s talking to each other with no router, no cloud, no ISP — wardriving instincts, pocket mesh, offline messaging. The foundation for every "what if it worked off-grid?" project.
→ numbpilled.gumroad.com/l/esp32phantom

Both live on numbpilled.gumroad.com — grab the one that matches the haunting you're building.

Clap 50x if your "quick weekend project" is now 6 months old and has a name. I see you.

articles.title: The Fenced Block Principle
articles.description: The problem: code that reads well but means something else   If you vibe code — or supervise...
articles.body_html:
The problem: code that reads well but means something else

If you vibe code — or supervise a coding agent that produces most of your diffs — you will have met the signature failure of AI-generated code. It compiles. It's idiomatic. The tests pass. And it implements a subtly different behaviour than the one you asked for, because the prompt was inexact or the model's reading of your codebase drifted.

Reviewers have a name for this: a correct answer to a slightly different question. It is the hardest class of defect to catch by reading code, because there is nothing wrong with the code. The wrongness lives one layer up, in the gap between what you intended and what the agent inferred.

The industry's current answer is spec-driven development (SDD): write the specification first, generate code against it, verify against it. That works, but it puts the spec upstream of the code as a contract, and once implementation begins, the two artefacts live separate lives. The spec becomes stale precisely when you need it most — at review time.

There is an older idea, and an older discipline, that suggests a different placement.

Knuth had the format; AI removes the burden

In 1984, Donald Knuth proposed literate programming. Instead of writing code with comments, you write a narrative document in which code appears as blocks embedded in prose explaining the intent. The code is extracted from the document ("tangling"); the document itself is the primary artefact.

Literate programming never went mainstream, and the reason is well understood: the parallel maintenance burden. Keeping prose and code synchronised by hand was exhausting, so most who tried it abandoned it despite conceding its benefits. Knuth's WEB system required manual tangling and weaving — constant friction.

That burden is exactly what coding agents remove. An LLM can regenerate the prose when the code changes, regenerate the code when the prose changes, and maintain both in lockstep without fatigue. The literate programming model — agents writing prose explaining intent for each executable block — is credible for precisely this reason. What killed the paradigm in 1990 is the thing agents are best at.

So the raw material exists: a 40-year-old format whose only fatal flaw has just been fixed. What's missing is the application of that format to mainstream, agent-generated Python and JavaScript — and, crucially, a recognised convention for using it.

The fenced block principle

The principle is simple to state:

Every block of code must be fenced with a corresponding statement of intent — either embedded in the same file or directly linked to one — and the pairing is a first-class, reviewable artifact.

Call it spec-anchored code at block granularity. The ingredients:

  1. Co-location or hard linkage. Intent lives with the code, not in a separate upstream document that decays. In practice, for mainstream languages, this means a convention like: every function, class, module or logical section is preceded by (or linked to) a fenced intent block — a short, plain-language statement of what this is supposed to do and why, written to be read by a human reviewer, not as an API docstring.
  2. Machine-enforceable pairing. A linter or CI check verifies that no code block exists without a matching intent block, and that stale pairings are flagged. The document is not decoration; its absence is a build failure.
  3. Parallel generation. The agent writes code and intent together, as parallel renderings of the same design. Critically — and this inverts the usual spec-driven relationship — clarifying the intent costs nothing. When a reviewer asks "did you mean this?", the agent revises the intent wording without touching the code. The intent becomes the cheap, conversational layer; the code becomes the expensive, verified layer.
  4. A side-by-side viewer. The review surface is not a diff of code. It is a two-pane view: intent on the left, code on the right, block by block. The reviewer's first question at every block is "does this code match this intent?" — and only then, "is this code correct?"

This last point is where the review economics change. Reviewing AI code by reading lines is expensive and demoralising at the volumes agents produce, which is why a third of PRs now ship with zero review. Reviewing intent is cheap: a wrong objective, a missing edge case, a misunderstood requirement — all of the "vibe" failures — are visible in a paragraph, long before they require line-by-line study of the implementation. The reviewer allocates line-reading only where the intent looks risky, and hands the rest to tests and verification.

What would need to exist for Python and JavaScript

None of this requires a new language. It requires conventions and tooling, and the tooling itself would, naturally, be built by AI. Sketching the minimum viable stack:

  • A pairing convention. The simplest credible form is structured comments or fenced blocks in the source file itself — for Python, an # intent: block above each definition; for JS/TS, a /** intent */ block distinct from JSDoc's @description API documentation. Intent is why and what-for; API docs are how to call. Conflating them is how intent documentation degrades into boilerplate.
  • An extractor/linter. A small tool (a tree-sitter pass, trivially agent-written) that parses a repo, builds the block-level intent/code index, and fails CI on unpaired code, orphaned intent, or pairings not updated when their code changed. Think ruff for intent.
  • Agent instructions. A clause for AGENTS.md obliging the agent to write and maintain the pairing — generate intent with code, update both on change, and ask the human to clarify intent wording rather than silently choosing an interpretation. This is where the clarification asymmetry pays: the conversation the agent should be having with you is about intent, not about implementation.
  • The viewer. A review UI (web or IDE panel) that renders the index side-by-side, highlights stale or divergent pairs, and lets the reviewer accept/reject at the level of "this code matches this intent" rather than line comments. Diff review then becomes the second pass, targeted where intent review found risk.
  • A drift signal. Because pairings are machine-checked, drift becomes measurable: the proportion of blocks whose intent was clarified or rewritten after generation is a direct, quantitative proxy for how much vibing happened in a codebase — a metric no current tooling gives you.

Existing systems prove the pieces work. AllSpeak, a coding system built along these lines, enforces the principle through its AGENTS.md and ships an editor/visualiser with the side-by-side view — demonstrating the format's feasibility, in the same way Knuth's WEB demonstrated literate programming's. Safety-critical engineering has enforced exactly this kind of linkage for decades: IEC 62304 and DO-178C both require traceable connections between requirements, design, code and tests. The fenced block principle is that discipline, made cheap enough for everyday vibe coding.

Objections, honestly

"The intent can be vibes too." Yes — if the agent writes both layers, a confabulated intent can sit beside confabulated code. Worse, the pair will be internally consistent, and a side-by-side view of two agreeing fictions is more dangerous than no viewer at all, because the agreement feels like verification and the reviewer never asks for a rewrite. The mitigation is the clarification loop: the intent layer only earns trust if the human has ratified it — which is far cheaper than ratifying code — and the viewer must visually distinguish agent-authored intent from intent the human has confirmed. Once that distinction exists, unratified blocks become a targeting mechanism: review starts where the intent is still a guess, not a promise.

"It catches the wrong objective, not the subtle bug." Correct. Intent review catches "correct answer to a slightly different question." It does not catch "slightly broken implementation of the right answer." For that you still need tests, verification, and targeted code reading. The claim is not that intent review replaces these — it's that it gives them a target and a budget. You read lines where the intent looked risky, and you let executable verification cover the rest.

"Block-level documentation is tedious." It was. When humans had to maintain it, it was tedious enough to kill literate programming. The entire bet of the principle is that agents change the maintenance cost curve — and a current revival of interest in literate programming suggests that bet is now worth taking.

The ask

None of the pieces above are hard to build any more; an agent could produce a working extractor, linter and viewer prototype in a long weekend. What's missing is the convention — agreement that intent, at block granularity, is a first-class artifact that mainstream AI tooling should carry alongside code.

If you build coding tools, the interesting open surface right now is not a better code generator. It's a better review target: tooling that lets a vibe coder see what the agent thought it was doing, block by block, before deciding whether to care how it did it.

The code is the deliverable — and it is usually a truthful implementation of the stated intent. That is exactly why the intent should be read first: when the code faithfully renders the wrong intent, it will compile, pass, and ship. Most of the bugs that matter live in the prose.

articles.title: Checking at compile time that arena memory can't escape its block
articles.description: Fels is a small systems language I've been building since June. It has no garbage collector. Memory...
articles.body_html:
Fels is a small systems language I've been building since June. It has no garbage collector. Memory lives in zones: arenas that are freed when their block ends. This post shows how the compiler makes sure nothing you allocate in a zone is used after the zone is gone, and where that check still has holes.

Why arenas need a check

An arena is the simplest allocator there is. It hands out memory from a big block by moving a pointer forward, and it frees everything at once at the end. There is no free per allocation, and allocating costs a few instructions.

The catch is the end. Once the arena is gone, every pointer into it dangles. In C or Zig nothing stops you from keeping one: you can return it, store it in a struct that lives longer, or hand it to a function that saves it. The program may even keep working until the memory is reused, and then it breaks somewhere else.

I wanted arenas without that catch, and without the weight of a full borrow checker.

Zones

A zone is an arena with a name and a block. Whatever you allocate in it lives until the block ends, and then all of it goes away in one step. You never call free, and nothing runs in the background.

#import std.io.{ println };

// The upper-case letters of `buf`, counted. It borrows `buf`: it may read and change it,
// but it cannot keep it.
count_upper :: fn(buf: borrow []u8) -> i32 {
    n: i32 = 0;
    for i in 0..buf.len {
        if buf[i] >= 'A' && buf[i] <= 'Z' { n += 1; }
    }
    return n;
}

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    total: i32 = 0;
    zone scratch: Arena {
        line := scratch.dupe(u8, "Fels Zones Are Arenas");
        total = count_upper(line);    // a borrow: fine
        first := line[0];             // a byte read out of the zone: a plain value
        total += first as i32 - 'F' as i32;
    }                                 // `line` is freed here
    println("{total} capitals");
    return total;
}

This prints 4 capitals. The copy of the text lives in scratch. count_upper may use it because its parameter says borrow. The count and the byte read out of the zone are plain numbers, so they are free to leave the block.

What the compiler refuses

There are three ways for zone memory to outlive its zone. Each one is a compile error.

Returning it.

// Copies `text` and makes its letters upper case.
shout :: fn(text: []const u8) -> []u8 {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        loud := scratch.dupe(u8, text);
        for i in 0..loud.len {
            if loud[i] >= 'a' && loud[i] <= 'z' { loud[i] -= 32; }
        }
        return loud;
    }
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot be returned
  --> ret.fels:8:9
  │
8 │         return loud;
  │         ^^^^^^^^^^^^

Storing it in something that lives longer.

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    keep: []u8 = .{};
    zone scratch: Arena {
        buf := scratch.new_slice(u8, 16);
        keep = buf;
    }
    return keep.len as i32;
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot escape its zone
  --> outer.fels:5:9
  │
5 │         keep = buf;
  │         ^^^^^^^^^^^

Passing it to a function that could keep it. println takes a plain slice, so nothing stops it from saving one. Only a borrow parameter promises not to.

#import std.io.{ println };

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        greeting := scratch.dupe(u8, "hello");
        println(greeting);
    }
    return 0;
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` can only be passed to a `borrow` parameter
  --> pass.fels:6:17
  │
6 │         println(greeting);
  │                 ^^^^^^^^

Ownership follows the value. A slice of zone memory, a field of it, and a struct built from it all belong to the zone too:

Line :: struct { text: []u8, number: i32 }

numbered :: fn(n: i32) -> Line {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        text := scratch.dupe(u8, "line");
        line: Line = .{ text, n };
        return line;    // error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot be returned
    }
}

The same goes for a borrow parameter itself. A function may read and change what it borrows, and pass it on to other borrow parameters, but it cannot return it:

first_word :: fn(text: borrow []u8) -> []u8 {
    i: usize = 0;
    while i < text.len && text[i] != ' ' { i += 1; }
    return text[0..i];    // error: borrowed value from `text` cannot be returned
}

How the check works

There are no lifetime annotations. The only word you ever write is borrow, on a parameter, never at a call. The check runs inside the type checker, one function at a time, with no extra pass.

For every value that holds zone memory, the checker keeps a small record: the zone that owns it, and how deeply nested the zone's block is. Everything else follows from a few rules:

  1. Allocating gives a value its owner. A call like scratch.dupe(...), scratch.new_slice(...) or scratch.alloc(...) on a zone handle returns memory owned by that zone.
  2. What you make from an owned value is owned too. A slice of it, a field of it, an element, a cast, an address taken from it, an if or match that may give it, a closure that captures it, and a struct or array literal that holds it all have the same owner. Only types that can carry a pointer carry an owner. A byte or a length read out of zone memory is a plain number, so it may go anywhere.
  3. An assignment passes the owner on. The variable the value lands in becomes owned by the zone as well. If that variable was declared outside the zone's block, it would outlive the memory, and that is the escape error.
  4. Returning an owned value is an error, and so is passing it to any parameter that is not borrow.
  5. A borrow parameter is an owner of its own kind. Inside the function the borrowed value can be read, changed and passed to other borrow parameters. It cannot be returned, stored through a pointer, or put into a global.

That is the whole idea: ownership belongs to names and scopes, not to types, so it costs almost nothing to check. The same machinery keeps a function from returning the address of one of its own locals, or storing it in a global.

What it does not catch

The check follows values through names, expressions and closures, but not through everything. Two roads stay open:

unsafe { addr = p as usize; }                     // a pointer turned into a number
register(fn() -> usize { return buf.len; });     // a closure handed to a function that keeps it

The first is what unsafe is for: a pointer turned into a number is just a number. The second is a trade-off. A function value cannot be a borrow parameter, so refusing every closure over zone memory as an argument would forbid comparators and callbacks too. A function that saves a closure it was given can carry zone memory past the zone.

Two more roads were open until this week: a value passed through an if or match expression, and a closure stored in a variable outside the zone. Writing this post turned them up, and both are compile errors now.

Try it

Fels is on GitHub at github.com/fels-lang/fels. The release download is for Windows; on Linux you build the compiler from source. The full rules for zones and borrow are in Memory and zones.

If you try it, I would love to hear where the check gets in your way, and where it lets something through that it should not.

articles.title: Don't Let the LLM Decide: How I Built a Predictable AI Tutor
articles.description: The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's...
articles.body_html:
The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's attempts and the answer. Tell it: "Help the learner, but don't give the answer away too early."

That works in a demo. It fails in an experiment. And it fails quietly in production too.

In the first post of this series I explained the experiment. I built an SQL tutor in two versions, called arms. Arm A makes you try before it helps, then gives a hint before the answer. Arm B gives the answer whenever you ask, like most AI tools. Six people used one or the other, then took a test a week later with no tutor.

This post is about how I built it. The core rule fits on one line:

The LLM never decides whether to help, or how much. Plain code decides. The LLM only writes the hint's wording, after that decision is made.

Why the LLM can't be the one deciding

Picture the prompt version. "If the learner seems stuck, give a hint. If they've really tried, give the answer."

Now try to answer one question: what did Arm A receive?

You can't. "Seems stuck" is a judgment the model makes fresh every time. Two learners in the same situation can get different help. The same learner can get different help on a retry. The thing you're trying to test becomes a moving target.

There's a second problem. With six people, there were only about 23 moments in the whole study where the tutor had to decide what help to give. You can't judge a model's decision-making from 23 examples. But you can fully test a plain function, and I did, with 123 unit tests.

So I split the system into three kinds of parts, a framing from my 100x Engineers AI course:

part does what why it sits there
human writes and runs SQL the skill being measured is theirs
deterministic (plain code) the try-first rule, the hint/answer rules, the answer checker, the leak guard the one thing being tested must be fixed and checkable
probabilistic (the LLM) writes the hint text, nothing else prose about this specific mistake is the one thing code can't write

The model is one small component. It's not the product.

The policy: a pure function

Here's the heart of policy.js, trimmed. No DOM, no network, no LLM. It takes the log for one question and returns an action.

const ACTION = {
  NONE:         'none',          // already solved
  REFUSE_GATE:  'refuse_gate',   // Arm A, no real attempt yet
  REFUSE_RETRY: 'refuse_retry',  // Arm A, hint given, keep trying
  HINT:         'hint',          // the LLM writes the text
  REVEAL:       'reveal',        // the reference query
};

const DEFAULT_N = 2; // attempts with the hint before the answer

function decide(item) {
  const N = item.N ?? DEFAULT_N;
  const counted = countableAttempts(item.attempts);
  const helpServed = item.helpServed || [];

  if (item.attempts.some(a => a.outcome === 'correct')) return { action: ACTION.NONE };

  // Arm B: the entire difference between the two groups is this line.
  if (item.arm === 'B') return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  // Arm A: the gate. No help of any kind until one attempt counts.
  if (counted.length === 0) return { action: ACTION.REFUSE_GATE };

  if (helpServed.some(h => h.action === ACTION.REVEAL)) return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  const hint = helpServed.find(h => h.action === ACTION.HINT);
  if (!hint) return { action: ACTION.HINT };

  const sinceHint = counted.length - hint.afterCountedAttempts;
  return sinceHint >= N ? { action: ACTION.REVEAL } : { action: ACTION.REFUSE_RETRY };
}

The only thing of interest here is the Arm B line. That one if is the whole difference between the two versions. Anyone can read it and know exactly what each group got.

Every decision is logged with counted and sinceHint. So for any Help press, I can look at the log and prove why the tutor responded the way it did.

N is fixed at 2 for everyone. If it changed per person, I'd be testing two things at once, and three people per group can't separate them.

What counts as an attempt?

Arm A's rule is "try first". I call it the gate: no help until you've made an attempt. So the code needs to decide what a real attempt is. This turned out to be the hardest part of the policy.

My first version said: an attempt counts if its result set is different from the last one. Simple, and wrong.

The bug: a query that doesn't run has no result set. So for a learner who couldn't get anything to execute, no attempt ever counted. The gate never opened. In my earlier test rounds, 101 of 122 attempts had a syntax error and didn't run. This wasn't an edge case. It was the main case.

And a query that fails to parse can still carry a full, wrong mental model:

SELECT customer, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 3

That doesn't run. It's also a perfect example of the exact mistake I was teaching about (filtering groups with WHERE instead of HAVING). It should count.

But asdf doesn't parse either. If junk counts, a learner can type three bits of junk and get a hint while thinking about nothing. Research on tutoring systems calls this "gaming the system", and learners find that shortcut fast.

So I added a substance bar. An attempt must contain one SQL keyword and one name from this question's schema:

function isSubstantive(sql, identifiers) {
  const low = String(sql ?? '').toLowerCase();
  if (!low.trim()) return false;
  if (!SQL_KEYWORDS.some(k => low.includes(k))) return false;
  if (!identifiers.length) return true; // fail open, see below
  return identifiers.some(id =>
    id.length >= 4
      ? low.includes(id)
      : new RegExp(`\\b${id}\\b`).test(low) // so "id" doesn't match "video"
  );
}

Matching is by substring on purpose. Real learners wrote GroupBy and havingcount>=3. That's mangled spelling, but a real mental model. A strict token match would throw those away.

I checked it against all 128 attempts from the screening round. 121 passed. The 7 rejected were 6 empty submissions and one bare SELECT. No real attempt was lost.

Notice the fail open line. If the schema list fails to load, the bar only checks for a keyword. A misconfigured page must not silently refuse every learner. That would turn Arm A into "no help at all" without anyone noticing.

The leak guard

Here's the uncomfortable part. To write a useful hint about a wrong query, the LLM has to see the correct one. I call that the reference query. So it's holding the answer while it writes. Sometimes it just prints it.

If that reaches the learner, Arm A quietly becomes Arm B on that question. The experiment stops testing anything, and nothing in the logs looks wrong.

So every hint passes through hint-guard.js before the learner sees it. It's deterministic. It makes no model calls. It looks at text and says yes or no.

function inspect(hint, { referenceQuery, learnerQuery }) {
  // 1. A runnable query: SELECT plus a real table after FROM/JOIN.
  // 2. A clause that distinguishes the reference query,
  //    unless the learner already wrote it themselves.
  // 3. Too much of the reference reproduced word for word.
  // 4. A walkthrough: four or more SQL keywords named.
}

If a hint is rejected, the system asks the model once more. If that fails too, it serves a hand-written fallback for that question. Every attempt and every rejection is logged.

Results: on 101 real hints, zero false alarms. Against 24 leaks I wrote specifically to beat it, it caught 22.

What can go wrong

Each rule in the guard exists because an earlier, simpler rule broke.

"SELECT and FROM means a leak." My first check rejected any hint containing both words. But they're normal English. "You started with SELECT, but where does the data come FROM?" is a great hint, and it got blocked. The fix: a runnable query must name a real table. The reference query tells you which tables exist, so look for those.

The semicolon rule. I also rejected "select ... ;" on the idea that a semicolon ends a statement. English uses semicolons too. "Nothing is processed; you need to say where the data comes from" got blocked. I deleted that rule instead of patching it, because the table rule already covered real queries.

Quoting the learner back to themselves. The prompt asks the model to quote what the learner wrote. So a hint would say "your MAX(price) is fine". MAX(price) is part of the answer, so the guard blocked it. 7 of 8 rejections in one test run were this. But the learner already wrote it. It's in their editor. Now a clause only counts as a leak if the learner doesn't already have it.

The leak with no SQL in it. "The FROM keyword picks the products table, then GROUP BY groups the rows by category..." No clause appears verbatim, but you could type the answer straight from it. The signal is shape, not content. A real hint talks about one or two things. A dictation names everything.

I didn't pick the threshold by feel. I measured it. Across the 101 real hints: 66 named no SQL keyword, 29 named one, 5 named two, 1 named three, and none named four. The two prose leaks named six and seven. A limit of four separates them with room on both sides.

The silent fallback. The LLM sits behind a Supabase edge function, so the API key never reaches the browser. Supabase pauses free projects after about a week without traffic. When paused, nothing errors. Arm A just serves the hand-written backup hints. The app looks fine, but it's quietly running a different tutor. I found this once, fixed it, and added a script to check it before every session.

What this means for your code

If you're putting an LLM into a product, ask one question about each decision: does this need judgment, or does it need to be the same every time?

  • If the behaviour has to be explainable, testable or consistent, it belongs in code.
  • If it needs language about this specific case, that's what the model is for.
  • Put a deterministic check between the model and the user for anything that would be expensive if the model got it wrong.

In my tutor, that split is why I could say exactly what each group got. It's also why the experiment could fail honestly. When two of my checks failed, I knew the failure was about learners, not about a model behaving differently on a Tuesday.

Next in the series: the mistakes I made running my first controlled experiment as a developer, including the one a Demo Day judge caught.

vikrantnegi / withholding-pilot

Learning OS — 100x Cohort 7 final capstone

Vikrant Negi. Solo. Demo Day track. Submission 7 Oct 2026.

An SQL tutor that makes you try before it helps, and a 6-person pilot testing whether that changes what you can do a week later, with the tutor gone.

For where things stand today, read STATUS.md. That is the only file that claims to be current.

Try it

Live app: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/

  • Withholding tutor: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/index.html?arm=A
  • Answer-giving baseline: https://tranquil-starlight-f0129e.netlify.app/index.html?arm=B

What each one does:

  • ?arm=A opens the withholding tutor. Press Help before trying, and it refuses. Try once, and Help gives a hint. Two more tries, and it gives the answer.
  • ?arm=B opens the baseline. Help gives the full answer at once.

Same page, same 16 practice questions, same grader. One config flag is the only difference.

The result

Arm A scored 36 of 36 person-questions (3 learners x 12 held-out questions). Arm…

articles.body_html:
Welcome to Day 1 of the public build log for HYNA-Stage.

For those catching up: We are HYNAWEB. I’m Harun (12-year-old Founder & CEO) and my co-founder is Akhouri (CTO). We are building enterprise-grade developer infrastructure entirely on a $150 Android phone using Termux.

Our mission with HYNA-Stage? Spin up isolated Firecracker microVMs in <5 seconds so AI agents have a safe, instant place to test code.

Today’s mission wasn’t about adding flashy features. It was about fixing the foundation: Authentication.

If users can’t log in smoothly, the product is dead. Here are the 3 "Boss Fights" we faced and conquered today to make HYNAWEB's auth flow bulletproof.

🐛 Boss Fight 1: The OAuth Hash Loop

  • The Symptom: Users clicked "Login with GitHub," authenticated successfully, but got dumped at the root URL (/#access_token=...) instead of the dashboard.
  • The Root Cause: Supabase rejected our redirectTo URL due to a hyphen mismatch (hynastage vs hyna-stage) in the configuration, falling back to the default Site URL and leaving the token stranded in the hash.
  • The Fix: I wrote a vanilla JS hash interceptor in index.html to instantly catch the token, forward it to dashboard.html, and parse it before the session timed out.

🐛 Boss Fight 2: The 401 JWT Gateway Block

  • The Symptom: Our custom CLI API keys were getting hit with 401 Unauthorized before even reaching the function logic.
  • The Root Cause: Supabase Edge Functions enforce JWT verification by default. It saw our custom CLI request, didn't recognize the JWT, and slammed the door.
  • The Fix: Disabled "Verify JWT with legacy secret" in the Supabase Edge Function settings, allowing our custom API key validation logic to run unimpeded.

🐛 Boss Fight 3: The RLS Permission Denied

  • The Symptom: Database queries returned 0 rows, even though the API key was valid.
  • The Root Cause: New Supabase projects require explicit Postgres GRANT permissions for the service_role, even when using the sb_secret_ bypass key. Row-Level Security was blocking the backend from reading its own table.
  • The Fix: Executed GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON TABLE public.api_keys TO service_role; in the SQL editor.

🏆 The Result

GitHub Auth is now live and buttery smooth. The redirect works perfectly. The CLI can talk to the database without getting blocked by the gatekeeper.

Today's HYNAWEB Stats:

  • Bugs squashed: 3
  • Auth flows perfected: 1
  • Laptops used: 0

Building cloud infrastructure on a mobile terminal means you don't have the luxury of bloat or easy debugging tools. Every fix has to be precise.

Tomorrow, we tackle the deployment pipeline and the Termux text-truncation nightmare.

Follow the series to see how we build the infrastructure for the AI era, one bash script at a time.

We are HYNAWEB. We don't just build apps; we build the future. 🐯☁️🚀

articles.title: Sending transactional email from Node.js in Ghana (and paying with mobile money)
articles.description: Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The...
articles.body_html:
Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The usual answer is SendGrid, Mailgun or Resend, and they're good services. But if you're building in Ghana, you hit the same wall I did: they're priced in dollars and want an international card.

So I built Sankofa, an email API that's prepaid in cedis. You top up with MTN MoMo, Telecel Cash or AirtelTigo Money at GHS 5 per 1,000 emails, with no subscription.

This post walks through sending email from a Node.js app with it, from your first test email to bulk sends and delivery webhooks.

1. Get an API key

Create an account, then open API Keys in the dashboard and create one. It starts with esk_ and is shown once, so put it straight into your environment:

export SANKOFA_API_KEY=esk_your_api_key

Keep it on your server. Never put it in frontend code, where anyone can read it.

2. Send your first email (no DNS needed)

Normally you can't send email until you've verified a domain. To get you going sooner, every account can use a shared test sender, hello@test.trysankofa.com, which can only send to the email address you signed up with:

const response = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "hello@test.trysankofa.com",
    to: "you@example.com", // the address you signed up with
    subject: "Hello from my app",
    text: "It works!",
  }),
});

const body = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${body.error}: ${body.message}`);
console.log("Sent:", body.messageId);

That uses the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later, so there's nothing to install. Check your inbox, and your spam folder the first time.

3. Send from your own domain

When you're ready to email your users, verify your domain on the Domains page. Sankofa gives you three DNS records to add. Once they're in, you can send from any address on that domain:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your order has shipped",
    html: "<p>Your order is on its way.</p>",
    text: "Your order is on its way.",
  }),
});

Each recipient uses one credit. If a send fails, the credit comes back automatically.

4. Templates, and sending to many people

For emails you send repeatedly, save a template with {{placeholders}}:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/templates", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    name: "order-shipped",
    subject: "Your order {{order}} has shipped",
    text: "Hi {{name}}, your order {{order}} is on its way.",
  }),
});

Then send it to up to 500 people in one request. Each person gets their own copy with their own values filled in:

const result = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails/bulk", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    templateName: "order-shipped",
    recipients: [
      { to: "ama@example.com", templateData: { name: "Ama", order: "A-1042" } },
      { to: "kofi@example.com", templateData: { name: "Kofi", order: "A-1043" } },
    ],
  }),
}).then((r) => r.json());

for (const r of result.results) console.log(r.to, r.status, r.error ?? "");

If one recipient fails (say, an address that bounced before), the rest still go out, and you're not charged for the failure.

5. Know when emails are delivered

Register a webhook on the Webhooks page, and Sankofa will POST delivery events to your server: delivered, bounced, opened, clicked and so on. Each request is signed, so check the signature before trusting it:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export function isFromSankofa(rawBody, signatureHeader, secret) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(signatureHeader.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")));
  if (!parts.t || !parts.v1) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) > 300) return false; // reject old requests

  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${parts.t}.${rawBody}`).digest();
  const given = Buffer.from(parts.v1, "hex");
  return given.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, expected);
}

Pass it the raw request body (before JSON parsing) and the X-Webhook-Signature header.

Bonus: let your AI assistant send email

Sankofa has an MCP server, so tools like Claude Code and Cursor can send email and check delivery for you. Create a separate API key for the agent and give it a daily limit, so it can never send more than you allow:

claude mcp add --transport http sankofa https://api.trysankofa.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer esk_your_agent_key"

Then you can ask, "email the team that the deploy is done", and it will.

Wrapping up

That covers most of what an app needs: test sends, your own domain, templates, bulk sends and delivery tracking. The docs cover the rest, including attachments and receiving replies.

It's early days, so I'd really value feedback, especially from anyone building in Ghana or elsewhere in West Africa. What do you use for email today, and what would make you switch?

The first 20 developers get 200 free emails to try it.

articles.title: Why Google Analytics breaks inside a Figma plugin, and what I built instead
articles.description: I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community...
articles.body_html:
I make Figma plugins. The numbers Figma gives me about them are installs and likes on the Community page. Neither one says whether anybody opened the plugin this week, or which of its buttons they pressed.

The usual answer on the web is Google Analytics. Paste the gtag snippet into a plugin's ui.html, open the console, and you get this:

SecurityError: Failed to read the 'cookie' property from 'Document':
Cookies are disabled inside 'data:' URLs.

The snippet is fine. The place it runs in is the problem, and that place turned out to be interesting enough that I ended up writing my own SDK for it. This post is about what I ran into.

A plugin is two programs

The first program is the main code, usually code.ts. It runs in a sandbox next to the document. It has the figma API and fetch. It has no DOM, no window and no document.

The second program is the UI. You pass an HTML string to figma.showUI(), and Figma loads that string into an iframe. The page gets a data: URL, so its origin is null.

Cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB all belong to an origin. A null origin owns none of them, and reading any of them throws. That is the error above.

The two programs cannot call each other. They talk through postMessage, and that is the only channel.

So the half that knows who the user is (the sandbox, through figma.currentUser) cannot see a click. The half that sees every click (the iframe) cannot remember anything and does not know who is clicking.

Web analytics assumes one page with a cookie jar. I had two halves and no jar.

Problem 1: the key is on one side, the buttons on the other

I wanted the developer to write the API key once. The sandbox is the right place for it, because the Figma data is there too:

// code.ts
import { tode } from '@tode-sdk/core';

figma.showUI(__html__);
await tode.init({ apiKey: 'your-api-key' });

init() reads the user id, the plugin id, the editor type (Figma, FigJam, Dev Mode, Slides) and posts all of it to the iframe in one message:

figma.ui.postMessage({ type: 'TODE_DATA', message: config });

The UI adapter listens for that message and configures itself. After that, both halves can send events with the same identity.

That is the happy path. It has a hole in it.

Problem 2: the first message gets lost

figma.showUI() returns before the iframe has loaded anything. If init() is fast and the UI bundle is slow, the config is posted to a page with no listener yet. Nobody hears it, the UI never becomes ready, and no error appears anywhere.

The same thing happens when a plugin closes its UI and calls showUI() again later. The new iframe starts empty.

The fix is a handshake that starts from the UI. When an adapter attaches its listener, it asks:

window.parent.postMessage(
  { pluginMessage: { type: 'TODE_UI_READY' }, pluginId: '*' },
  '*',
);

The sandbox answers by posting the config again. One detail matters here. Most plugins already set figma.ui.onmessage for their own messages, and assigning it a second time would overwrite their handler. figma.ui.on('message', ...) adds a listener next to it and leaves theirs alone, so the SDK uses that.

The plugin's own handler still receives the TODE_UI_READY message. It has to ignore message types it does not know, which a well-written handler does anyway.

Problem 3: events that fire before the SDK is ready

A common first event is "plugin opened". It fires on mount, before the config has crossed over from the sandbox.

My first version told developers to wrap every call in if (isReady). That is a rule people forget, and the event they lose is the most important one.

Now the SDK keeps early events in a queue with the time they happened, and sends them when the config arrives:

if (this._isReady && this._apiKey) {
  await this.send(event);
  return;
}
if (this._queue.length >= MAX_QUEUED_EVENTS) return; // 50
this._queue.push(event); // event.timestamp was set at call time

The cap is 50. If something calls trackAction in a loop while the SDK is not ready, I would rather drop events than grow an array forever inside someone else's plugin.

Problem 4: how long is a session

On a website, session length comes from page views with timestamps and a timeout. A plugin has no pages. It has a panel that is open for a while and then is gone.

I did not want to depend on an unload event firing in an iframe that Figma can remove at any moment. So I turned the question around. The UI opens a WebSocket when it becomes ready and holds it. The server writes down when the socket opened. When the socket closes, for any reason, the server writes one session row with the duration.

A closed panel, a closed tab and a crashed browser all look the same to the server: the socket is gone. No goodbye message is needed.

The client sends ping every 5 seconds. If the server hears nothing for 60 seconds, it ends the session itself, so a dead connection cannot inflate the numbers.

That covers a panel someone opens and closes. Three other cases needed more work.

The first is laptop sleep. People leave a plugin open, close the lid and come back hours later. The socket is dead and the panel is still on screen. The SDK reconnects with backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, capped at 30s) and never gives up while the UI is open. It also listens for the browser's online event and retries at once when the network is back.

The second follows from the first. Each reconnect is a new session row on the server. Every connection carries the same session_id, generated once per UI load, so the rows can be grouped later.

The third is React. Five components calling useTode() used to mean five sockets and five sessions for one person. The socket is now shared and reference-counted. The first caller opens it, and it closes when the last holder is gone.

Problem 5: analytics must never break the plugin

If my server is down, a designer's export button still has to work. So nothing in the SDK throws. init() and trackAction() catch everything and log to the console.

The sandbox made this harder than I expected. It has fetch, and it has no AbortController. Its fetch ignores signal. A request that hangs cannot be cancelled there, which means await tode.init() could block a plugin's startup.

The workaround is a race against a timer:

if (typeof AbortController === 'undefined') {
  const timeout = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timed out')), 10_000);
  });
  return Promise.race([fetch(url, rest), timeout])
    .finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

The request itself may still be hanging somewhere. The plugin has stopped waiting for it, and that is the part I care about.

Counting people without a cookie

A cookie exists on the web because the page does not know who you are. A plugin does. figma.currentUser.id is stable for a Figma account, and you get it by adding one line to the manifest:

{
  "permissions": ["currentuser"],
  "networkAccess": {
    "allowedDomains": [
      "https://processing.usetode.dev",
      "wss://processing.usetode.dev"
    ]
  }
}

That id is enough to tell a new user from a returning one, which is where retention comes from. The SDK sends the id and nothing else about the person: no name, no email, no file contents.

Country is looked up on the server from the request IP. The IP is not stored.

Without the currentuser permission, figma.currentUser is null. The SDK sends an empty value in that case and events still arrive. You lose unique users and keep everything else.

What it looks like from the plugin side

After all of that, the part a plugin developer writes is small:

import { useTode } from '@tode-sdk/figma-react';

function ExportButton() {
  const { trackAction, trackActionWithMetric } = useTode();

  const onExport = async () => {
    const layers = await exportSelection();
    trackAction('export_clicked');
    trackActionWithMetric('layers_exported', layers.length);
  };

  return <button onClick={onExport}>Export</button>;
}

There are adapters for React, Vue, Angular, Svelte and plain TypeScript. They are thin. The queue, the handshake and the socket all live in the core package, so I only fix each bug once.

What I have not solved

There is no way to learn from plugin code that an event failed to deliver. Failures go to console.error and that is all. I chose silence over callbacks because I did not want analytics error handling in people's plugins, and I am still not sure it was the right call.

Sessions need a UI. A plugin that runs a command with no panel has no iframe to hold a socket, so it gets events and no session length.

And a reconnect still shows up as a separate row on the server. The shared session_id makes it fixable, and I have not built the merge yet.

If you want to look at the code

The SDK is MIT licensed and lives at github.com/kolebayev/tode-sdk. The service behind it is tode. It has a free plan for one plugin, and the paid plans are how I cover the servers.

If you came here for the Google Analytics error and want the long answer, I wrote up what the Measurement Protocol can and cannot do inside a plugin.

I would like to hear from people who build extensions for other hosts, like VS Code, Chrome or Sketch. How do you find out whether anyone uses what you shipped?

articles.title: typescript-eslint suggests void. With supabase-js, that drops the request.
articles.description: For the first 39 sends of a new feature in a production app I run, open tracking just didn't work....
articles.body_html:
For the first 39 sends of a new feature in a production app I run, open tracking just didn't work. The sends went out fine. The opens never got recorded: 39 sends recorded zero opens. No exception, nothing in the logs, every test green. It came down to one word.

The call looked roughly like this (names changed):

void supabase.rpc('track_event', { id });

That void was a habit. typescript-eslint's no-floating-promises complains about promises you don't await, and its message tells you to await it, handle it, or have it "explicitly marked as ignored with the void operator". The first suggestion it offers is "Add void operator to ignore." For an eager promise, like a storage upload or an auth call, that's fine, because the request is already on its way.

A supabase-js query builder isn't like that. It's a lazy thenable, and nothing gets sent until something calls .then() on it. await does that for you. void doesn't. So void supabase.rpc(...) builds the request and then throws it away.

It gets worse. Since typescript-eslint 8.0.0, no-floating-promises doesn't check thenables by default, so a builder you forgot on its own line isn't flagged by anything. And if you turn checkThenables on to catch those, the rule flags every builder and suggests void first, which is the one fix guaranteed to make sure the request never happens.

So I built an ESLint plugin that knows the difference: eslint-plugin-supabase. It has five rules, each for a Supabase mistake that's easy to ship without noticing. Four of them don't produce an error at all.

1. The query that never gets sent

supabase/no-unsent-query flags a lazy builder that's voided or just left sitting there as a statement:

void supabase.from('todos').insert({ title }); // voided: never sent
supabase.from('todos').update({ done: true }).eq('id', id); // never awaited: never sent

You get two suggestions, await (inside an async function) and .then(). There's no autofix, because both change when the request runs, and that's your call to make. .then() chains, await, return and passing the builder somewhere else are all fine. Storage downloads are lazy too, so they're covered.

2. The subscription that never fires 

supabase
  .channel('room')
  .on('postgres_changes', { event: 'INSERT', schema: 'public', table: 'messages' }, onMessage)
  .subscribe((status) => console.log(status));

If public.messages isn't in the supabase_realtime publication, this channel happily reaches SUBSCRIBED and then never gets a single event. The only error is a system message your subscribe callback never sees. That same app had a subscription like this sitting on an unpublished table while the table took 1,926 writes. It fired zero times.

supabase/realtime-table-published replays your migrations and reports the subscription, along with the fix: alter publication supabase_realtime add table public.messages;.

3. The read that comes back empty 

const { data, error } = await supabase.from('orders').select('*');
// data: [], error: null

If public.orders has row level security on and no select policy for the role your client uses, this read gives you an empty result and no error. An update or delete in the same situation quietly changes nothing, also without an error. (Inserts and upserts fail loudly with 42501, so the rule doesn't bother with them.)

supabase/rls-readable reads your policies from the migrations and reports the read, plus filtered updates and deletes.

4. The channel error nobody hears 

supabase.channel('room').on('broadcast', { event: 'ping' }, onPing).subscribe();

Call .subscribe() without a status callback and CHANNEL_ERROR and TIMED_OUT go nowhere. supabase/subscribe-status-handler asks you to pass one: .subscribe((status, err) => { ... }). If you already wrap subscribe in a helper that checks the status, add it to allowWrappers.

5. The call the 2026-10-30 change will break

This one comes with a date, so it gets its own section further down.

Why a linter needs your schema

Supabase's own database linter already catches something close to the empty read (the third one above): lint 0008_rls_enabled_no_policy flags every table with row level security on and no policy. But plenty of those tables are like that on purpose. The app only reads them through a function, and "no policy" is the design.

You can't tell a deliberate table from a broken one by looking at the database alone. You can't tell from the client code alone either: supabase.from('orders').select() looks fine until you know what the migrations say about orders. You need both. So the schema rules replay supabase/migrations into a model of the database (tables, grants, row level security, policies, publication membership) and check every client call against it. A table that's only read through a function never trips rls-readable, because there's no direct client call to report.

The plugin also works out which role each client acts as. A client created with a publishable or anon key is anon or authenticated. A client created with the service role key bypasses row level security, so rls-readable leaves it alone. When the plugin can't trace a client at all, it skips the call and counts the skip. When it can trace the client but can't tell what kind of key it got (createClient(url, config.key)), it treats it like a publishable client by default (unknownKey: "default"), because in client code that's almost always what it is. Set unknownKey: "skip" if you'd rather skip those calls.

2026-10-30: find the call sites before the change does

Supabase has announced that from 2026-10-30, new tables, views and sequences in public stop getting automatic grants for anon, authenticated and service_role on every existing project. A migration that creates a table and forgets the grant will apply cleanly, row level security will look right, and the first request will fail.

After the change, a client call on a new table that the role has no grant for fails with 42501. supabase-grants-lint catches it at the migration. This plugin catches it at the line of client code that will break. A Realtime subscription on such a table fails silently instead: it connects and never receives any data.

supabase/table-granted knows which privileges each call needs (an upsert needs insert, update and select; a filtered delete needs delete and select) and reports a call when no role the client can act as has them:

authenticated has no insert privilege on `public.orders` in your migrations, so this call fails with
42501 (permission denied). Fix in a migration: `grant insert on public.orders to authenticated;`

Right now, before the change, the replayed defaults still grant almost everything, so this rule is quiet on most projects. And the replay doesn't look at the calendar. It only sees the change once your project records it, either with the opt-in migration (the revoke SQL Supabase published) or with grants-lint's since setting. Without one of those, the rule stays quiet after 2026-10-30 too. Once it's recorded, every table your next migration creates gets checked at the call site, in your editor, before the request fails in production.

What it found in 99 public repos

I ran the recommended config over 99 public repositories that have Supabase migrations, TypeScript sources and supabase-js. I pinned the commits and linted them as they are. Out of those 99:

  • 35 of 99 (35.4%) had at least one finding.
  • 15 of 99 (15.2%) subscribed with postgres_changes to a table their migrations never add to the publication.
  • 11 of 99 (11.1%) had a read, update or delete that row level security turns into a silent no-op, by their own migrations.
  • 8 of 99 (8.1%) had a query that's never sent, either voided or left floating.
  • 29 of 99 (29.3%) had a .subscribe() with no status callback.
  • 2 of 99 (2.0%) already had a call with no privilege behind it, before the change.

Some honest caveats. The corpus only sees migrations, so a table published or a policy added by hand in the dashboard is invisible to it, and a finding can be right about the migrations and still not happen in that repo's production database. It's not a random sample of Supabase apps either. Calls the plugin can't resolve are skipped, so treat these numbers as lower bounds. I also did a blind hand review of 50 schema findings, drawn at random from a fresh run I hadn't looked at before. It turned up 2 false positives (4.0%), and one of those came from my own corpus harness and is fixed. I'm not naming any of the repositories, and I won't.

Try it

You'll need a TypeScript project with typed linting:

npm install --save-dev eslint-plugin-supabase eslint @typescript-eslint/parser "typescript@>=5.8 <6.1"

// eslint.config.mjs
import parser from '@typescript-eslint/parser';
import supabase from 'eslint-plugin-supabase';

export default [
  {
    files: ['**/*.ts', '**/*.tsx'],
    ignores: ['**/supabase/functions/**'],
    languageOptions: {
      parser,
      parserOptions: { projectService: true, tsconfigRootDir: import.meta.dirname },
    },
  },
  supabase.configs.recommended,
];

Then run npx eslint .. The ignores line keeps Deno edge functions out of typed linting. The two code rules work on any project. The three schema rules look for supabase/migrations next to your code (and read grants-lint.config.json if you have one). If you created your tables in the dashboard, run supabase db pull once so your migrations actually create them. The plugin doesn't open a network connection, doesn't read your .env file and doesn't send telemetry.

One more step for the 2026-10-30 change. Once your project is past it (or you opted in early from the dashboard), tell the replay: add the opt-in migration (the revoke SQL Supabase published), or set since in grants-lint.config.json to the version of your last migration before the change. Without one of those, the replay keeps the old automatic grants and table-granted stays quiet on new tables.

How I built it

The schema rules don't parse SQL themselves. They use the replay engine from supabase-grants-lint, the migration linter I wrote for the same change, through a new engine export. That way the CLI and the editor agree on what your migrations mean.

Before writing this, I pointed the plugin at the history of the app where both incidents happened. At the commit before the void fix, no-unsent-query reports the call. At the fix, it goes quiet. The subscription was harder. That app adds tables to the publication inside a do block, which a replay can't read, so the plugin skips those subscriptions instead of guessing (reportUnresolved names the block and asks for plain alter publication statements). With the block rewritten as plain statements, realtime-table-published reports the unpublished subscription and nothing else.

Every guard in the rules is mutation-tested, and every rule has a test for each case it leaves alone on purpose.

It doesn't check the 1,000-row PostgREST limit. For that, use rowcap by anabecalab, which does it well.

Try it on your project

Run it once before 2026-10-30. If it finds something, or flags something that isn't a bug, please open an issue. A false positive is a bug, and I want to fix it this week.

I used AI to help draft and edit this post; the plugin, the tests and the numbers are mine.
